observations by XMM [1] and compare it with the previously published map based
on 4 years of data [2]. We investigate the spatial structure of the main
features, such as the polar diffuse bands and the equatorial bright band, and
we quantify their characteristics in terms of intensity, width, and
position. We also study the spectral properties of the XMB in the 0.5-10 keV
band through the analysis of the spectrum extracted from the total map and from
maps binned in intensity intervals. The main findings of this work are: i) the
new XMB map is more complete in intensity, especially at high latitudes, due
to the increased exposure; ii) the properties of the polar diffuse bands are
consistent with a torus geometry; iii) the equatorial bright band is wider and
brighter in the intensity map than in the exposure map, suggesting that it is
not only a feature of the cosmic X-ray background but also of the diffuse
background; iv) the spectrum of the total map is consistent with that of the
cosmic X-ray background, while the spectrum of the map in the intensity
interval 1e-6-1e-5 cm^{-2}s^{-1} is harder than that of the total map; v) the
spectrum of the low-intensity maps is softer than the cosmic X-ray background
spectrum; vi) the emission mechanism of the XMB is still unknown.
  Finally, we discuss the new results in the light of the current knowledge on
the XMB and we highlight the open questions that a more detailed analysis of
the new XMM-Newton Diffuse Background map could provide.

a low mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 11.8%. The proposed approach
could be used as a performance benchmark for evaluating new protocols or
mechanisms in a cellular network.

entire 3 days of field-trial data is used. In contrast, most existing
simulations use a few hundred sessions, which is not sufficient to capture
the high periodicity of the session establishment rates. To further validate
our approach, we use the field-trial data to simulate 1000 sessions and
compare the results with the predictions of the model. The simulated and
predicted session establishment rates match very well with a MAPE of 12.3%.
This tells us that the model is not only validated by the testing data but
also reflects the behavior of 1000 sessions in the network.

Linear Collider (ILC) that were validated in 2012 SiD features a compact,
cost-constrained design for precision Higgs and other measurements, and
sensitivity to a wide range of possible new phenomena. The final focus system
(FFS) plays a crucial role in the overall detector design. With a beam spot size
of only about 0.5 nm x 30 nm, the FFS must provide precise position and angle
measurements for the two beams, with a collision point (IP) location accuracy
of about 50 $\mu$m in all three dimensions. The FFS includes the final focus
magnets, tracking detectors, and support infrastructure. The tracking system
includes five large area vertex detectors (VDX) surrounding the interaction point
and eight main tracking systems (MTX) in the solenoid regions at a radius between
3 and 4 meters. The MTX detectors operate in a region of high momentum where
separation between charged and neutral particles is less important, but precise
measurement of transverse momentum in the laboratory frame is critical. The
design of the MTX includes large area, high resolution, double-layer tracking
layers with a mix of pixel and strip sensors. The operational characteristics
and expected performance of the MTX detectors will be presented.
  Finally, the integration of the FFS into the overall SiD detector will be
discussed.

a systematic study of the properties of the
compact remnant of binary neutron star mergers using long-wavelength numerical
simulations. We have explored the dependence of the merger outcome on the
orientation of the binary total angular momentum, by considering three different
values of the inclination of the spins of the two compact objects with
respect to their total angular momentum. We have also investigated how the
merger dynamics is affected by the presence of magnetic fields in the neutron
stars, by considering two different magnetization scenarios and by implementing
a simple model for the simulation in which the magnetic fields play a key
role in breaking the neutron-star interiors and altering the gravitational
interaction between the two compact objects. Finally, we have also varied the
equation of state (EOS) of dense matter by considering different relativistic
toy-EOSs, to explore how the merger dynamics is affected by the compressibility
of the neutron-star matter. By considering these different initial conditions,
we have explored the variety of outcomes that can be obtained in the context of
magnetic, spinning, and eccentric binary mergers, and we have investigated how
the presence of magnetic fields can influence the interaction between the two
compact objects. We have also investigated the possible impact of the magnetic
fields on the formation of a global magnetar-like magnetic field in the remnant
and on the production of the neutrinos and the electromagnetic signals
associated to the merger.
  In this abstract, we focus on the main features of the different simulations
that we have performed. We have explored how the orientation of the binary
angular momentum changes the merger dynamics and we have investigated the
possible formation of a global magnetic field in the remnant. In the
orientation that we have dubbed "perpendicular" the neutron-star matter is
strongly broken and the magnetic fields play a key role in the simulation. In
the "near-aligned" simulation the magnetic fields are also relevant, even if
the matter is less broken. In the "aligned" simulation the magnetic fields are
slightly relevant and in the "antiparallel" simulation they are not relevant at
all. In the three simulations in which the magnetic fields are relevant we have
observed a strong reduction of the matter ejection and a more efficient
formation of a torus. The main difference between the "perpendicular" and
"near-aligned" simulations is the level of fragmentation of the matter and the
amount of energy carried away by the neutrinos.

of the massive spin-2 particle, which resolves the paradox.

boundary dilaton becomes a dynamical variable, as proposed by Verlinde. The
difference with their approach, however, is that the role of the modular
string is played by the graviton, which is a purely holographic object. This
implies that the picture can be extended to resolve the black-hole puzzle in

\textit{adaptive} adversary who can arbitrarily corrupt the reward and
transition at every step within an episode, for at most $\epsilon$-fraction of
the learning episodes. Our attack model is stronger than that considered in the
existing literature (e.g., \alp@conf/NeurIPS/2020/RobustRL; zang et al.
\@conf/NeurIPS/2022/R3RL). Our defense model is also stronger than that in
\alp@conf/NeurIPS/2020/RobustRL, as we assume the adversary has infinite attack
budget. Our goal is to compute the robust performance of the policy that is
secure against such an adversary. To compute this robust performance, we
propagate an upper bound on the robust episode reward to the central controller
via a reverse Bellman operator that takes an $\epsilon$-fraction of adversarial
corruption across episodes. Our proposed robust Bellman operator enables to
compute the robust performance of any given policy using a single learning
episode. We utilize this operator to develop a robust value iteration algorithm
that can compute an optimal policy using $\mathcal{O}(HSA/\epsilon)$ episodes,
where $H$ is the episode length. Our algorithm uses $\mathcal{O}(SA/\epsilon)$
sample queries to the unknown transition and reward, where $S$ is the number of
states. The sample complexity of our algorithm improves $SA/\epsilon$ from the
existing robust Q-learning algorithm \alp@conf/NeurIPS/2020/RobustRL. We also
develop a robust policy optimization algorithm that can optimize the universal
policy function using $\mathcal{O}(HSA/\epsilon)$ episodes, where $A$ is the
number of actions. The sample complexity of our algorithm improves $SA/\epsilon$
from the existing robust policy optimization algorithm \alp@conf/NeurIPS/2020/RobustRL.

adaptive grid world environment.

how well this framework can reconstruct topological features from partial

of reconstructing from partial information the topological features of
networks with given degree distributions. Specifically, we consider the
topological features of the percolation and bootstrap percolation phenomena
that occur in networks with given degree distributions. We show that the
thresholds of the percolation phase transitions and the exact values of the
bootstrap percolation thresholds can be obtained by considering only a small
fraction of the nodes of the network. However, the rough estimate of the
percolation thresholds obtained from the largest degree in the network can also
be accurate for a small fraction of nodes. We also show that the phenomenon of
a sharp transition from a finite to infinite bootstrap percolation threshold
with increasing degree centralization can be lost in networks with a small
fraction of high-degree nodes.

the mixing properties of networks, such as their clustering coefficients. We
show that the mixing of a network can be highly over- or under-estimated from
even a large fraction of the local clustering around individual nodes. However
the average clustering coefficient of a network can be accurately estimated from
a large fraction of nodes.

information the assortativity of a network. We show that the degree-degree
correlation of a network can be highly over- or under-estimated from even a
large fraction of the nodes. However, the average degree-degree correlation of
a network can be accurately estimated from a large fraction of nodes.

all of the topological features of a network from even a small fraction of the
network's nodes. We also show that some of the reconstructed features may be

extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) has been studied for over
three decades. Despite the fact that NER has achieved great success with
neural-network-based approaches, it still suffers from data sparsity and
insufficient domain generalization. The first issue stems from the fact that
high-quality annotated datasets are expensive to obtain and typically contain
only a few categories or are dominated by a few well-represented classes. The
second issue is due to the fact that pre-trained language models, which have
become a cornerstone in modern NER systems, usually have limited domain
generalization ability. To tackle these challenges, we propose a unified
framework that simultaneously resolves data sparsity and domain generalization
for NER. Specifically, we introduce a novel domain-adaptive pre-training
strategy for NER, termed as DAMER, which jointly adapts both the model and
domain-specific data. To achieve this, we propose a novel domain-aware
adversarial training strategy that optimizes the model using a domain-specific
mini-batch-wise adversarial loss. We further introduce a domain-aware
evaluation strategy to evaluate NERS by using a target domain's data. Our
experiments show that DAMER achieves the best performance on both generalizing
to unseen domains and resolving data sparsity compared to state-of-the-art
state-of-the-art methods.
  We also conduct an extensive set analysis on commonly used NER datasets.
Interesting observations are that 1) the performance on the most frequent
categories is usually much higher than that on less frequent ones and 2) the
performance on categories in the primary domain is usually much higher than
that on categories in the cross-domain. Our analysis provides a new perspective
on the issue of data sparsity in NER and shows that existing methods do not
fully address this problem.

accurate information on this topic through unstructured web search, but are
completely successful through fact-checking specific web search. Our analysis
shows that this is not because fact-checking specific search queries return
different and more accurate results, but because it causes users to filter out
highly authoritative and accurate pages. This observation highlights the need
for search interfaces that are able to effectively filter out low-quality
information, regardless of whether that information is accurate or not.

designed to help users find accurate information. Through another user study,
we show that this interface is able to significantly improve the accuracy of
web search for factual errors, even in the presence of misinformation.

problem of low digital literacy, but also a problem of search. It presents
new insights into how users search for and find accurate information on
newsworthy topics. And it presents a novel interface for fact-checking web

resilience of distribution systems after disruptions. We consider a test network
and quantify the potential benefits of EVs in terms of restoration time and
energy supplied. We also consider two restoration strategies: a centralized
optimization model and a decentralized iterative model based on which prices are
updated based on an auction mechanism. We compare the two approaches and evaluate
the level of decentralization in the decentralized model. We also explore the
impact of information availability on the two approaches. In the centralized
model, we consider three scenarios: (1) a centralized optimizer has full
information, (2) a centralized optimizer has partial information, and (3) no
centralized optimizer (i.e., no information is available). We find that the
decentralized model with partial information performs the best in terms of
restoration time.
  We also find that EVs can reduce the restoration time by up to 50% and
improve the energy supplied by up to 30% after disruptions. We find that in the
decentralized model, EV owners and non-EV owners have different pay-off functions
and thus may behave differently. We find that EV owners are more willing to
wait for their homes to be restored and are less likely to disconnect from the
network. We also find that non-EV owners are more likely to disconnect from the
network if they have priority in restoration.
  Our results show that private EVs can enhance the resilience of distribution
systems. The decentralized model provides a framework for decision-making in a
multi-agent setting. The level of decentralization can be tuned based on the
information available and the level of coordination desired among agents.
Information availability is crucial for both centralized and decentralized
approaches.
  Finally, our work provides a framework for further research. We can extend
our models to include other distributed energy resources (DERs) and investigate
their effects on the resilience of distribution systems. We can also investigate
the impact of EV charging policies on the resilience of distribution systems and
provide a link between DER policy and system performance.

controllers and DIMM configurations.

configurations including single-rank, multi-rank, and multi-DIMM systems. To
evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed interconnect architecture, we
demonstrate that it can support a number of advanced memory features including
core and memory scrubbing, refresh, and thermal monitoring. The results show

In this paper, we consider the multi-agent extension of the Motivation Dynamics
framework and show how the resulting system can encode persistent team
affiliations and collective boundary behaviors. We analytically characterize
the bifurcation structure of the resulting system, show how it encodes persistent
team affiliations, and discuss how it can be used to encode various types of
collective behaviors.
  We then consider a control-theoretic formulation of an obstacle avoidance
problem, in which a team of agents avoid colliding with each other and with
stationary obstacles whose positions are unknown. We show how the multi-agent
Motivation Dynamics framework can be used to encode this behavior, and
illustrate the resulting system through numerical simulations.
  The resulting system encodes a number of desirable properties, including
fast and robust collision avoidance, collective boundary behaviors, and the
ability to circumnavigate the unknown positions of stationary obstacles. We
illustrate the effectiveness of this approach through numerical simulations and
show how it compares to a number of alternative approaches to autonomous
navigation.
  Finally, we note that the underlying control-theoretic formulation of this
problem is based on a "negative" approach to obstacle avoidance, in which the
agents are motivated to avoid collisions through the presence of repulsive
potentials that are generated by the obstacles themselves. We discuss how this
formulation could be extended to a "positive" approach, in which the agents are
motivated to make contact with stationary obstacles in order to "anchor" their
positions, and how such an approach could be used to improve the overall
navigation performance of the team.

potential to improve the safety and effectiveness of autonomous mobile agents,
and to provide a number of new tools for the specification and control of
multi-agent systems.

designed to address these and other specification needs.

a new type of dark matter halos,
named ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs), through high-resolution observations of
their stellar kinematics and stellar populations. UDGs are extremely diffuse
($r_e$ > 1.5 kpc), low-mass (L < L$^{*}$), and low-surface-density galaxies,
mainly found in the outskirts of dense galaxy clusters. Their nature is still
poorly understood, and several scenarios have been proposed, ranging from
dark-matter poor systems that are able to maintain a large size due to
suppressed baryonic collapse to the near-proto-universal density models, with a
high dark matter content and a very low star formation efficiency. Here we
present the analysis of the stellar kinematics and stellar populations of six
UDGs, observed with the Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS) VLT/X-Shooter. We
discuss the properties of their kinematic and spectroscopic parameters, and
compare them to those of high-surface-density galaxies, both in the field and
in clusters. We find that UDGs have a wide range of kinematic and
spectroscopic properties, and we are able to separate them into two classes:
those with a low stellar mass and a low [Z/H] (low-mass low-z UDGs), and those
with a higher stellar mass and a higher [Z/H] (high-mass high-z UDGs). The
low-mass low-z UDGs are consistent with systems with a very low star formation
efficiency, and are likely to be near-proto-universal density systems. The
high-mass high-z UDGs, on the other hand, are consistent with systems with a
low star formation efficiency and a low dark matter fraction, and are likely
to be the faint extension of the high-surface-density galaxy population.
Finally, we note that the distinction between low-mass low-z and high-mass
high-z UDGs is crucial, and it is related to the definition of the UDG population
itself.

sensitive task? Deep
object detectors exploit scene context for recognition, but their performance
varies on different datasets. We observe that the performance of object
detectors is strongly correlated with their robustness to out-of-domain objects.
Existing object detectors not only fail to localize difficult objects but also
extract noisy information from the background, resulting in the inclusion of
indirect context. To study the relationship between object detectors and
contextuality, we propose a unified framework that integrates object detectors
with out-of-distribution generalization power into a single axis. We include 12
state-of-the-art object detectors and evaluate them based on their context
sensitivity. Our results show that object detectors can be grouped into three
clusters based on their context sensitivity: low, medium, and high. Low cluster
detectors are robust to both difficult and out-of-domain objects. We observe
that medium and high context sensitivity detectors are better at exploiting
context, but also introduce more background noise. We find that the medium
cluster is the most suitable for balance between robustness and context
sensitivity. We also observe that increasing the capacity of high sensitivity
detectors does not lead to better performance. Our analysis shows that high
sensitivity is an artifact of overfitting. We propose a simple capacity
regularization technique that can be used to evaluate the context sensitivity
of object detectors.
  Our framework provides a unique perspective on object detectors and can be
used to evaluate and compare object detectors on context sensitivity. It can
also be used to evaluate the effect of different techniques on context
sensitivity and can be used to evaluate the performance of end-user applications
that require object detection with varying context.

Poisson multi-Task learning (MTL) framework
that allows for a task-represented variance covariance matrix. This is
particularly useful when the variance covariance matrix is task-dependent and
is in a high dimensional setting. We propose a framework that uses a matrix
factorization based approach to learn a block-diagonal variance covariance
structure. This allows for a low dimensional representation of the variance
covariance matrix. We show that our approach is not only computationally
efficient but also provides a sparse solution when the data is sampled from a
sparse graph. We provide a theoretical result showing that with a sufficiently
large number of samples, our algorithm is able to recover the underlying graph
structure. We perform experiments on both synthetic and real world datasets.
The results show that our framework outperforms the baseline MTL methods.
Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a sparse solution with a closed
form solution for the Poisson MTL setting.

formulas of the typed system as constraints on word lemmas representing

type of a set of word lemmas together with a semantic annotation in terms of a

composition function that computes semantic annotations of syntactic combinations

proof of conservativity of modality. The system is applied to a morphological
tagging task where words are tagged with parts of speech together with their

exact ergodic capacity (EC) of a
point-to-point multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system assisted by an
intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). In order to take into account the
nonlinearity of the amplitude of the composite channel, we assume a general
form for the distribution of the observation at the receiver. To this end, we
derive an expression for the EC that does not require any specific distribution
of the observation at the receiver, but only the knowledge of the moment-generating
function (MGF) of the observation or the knowledge of the probability density
function (PDF) of the observation for a special case. We show that the EC
optimization problem is challenging due to the coupling between the channel
parameters and the reflection coefficients vector, which results in a non-convex
problem with respect to the aforementioned vector. In order to tackle this
difficulty, we propose an optimization algorithm based on an alternating convex
concentration algorithm that successfully decouples the above-mentioned
coupling. Moreover, the proposed optimization algorithm does not require the
inverse of the Hessian matrix of the EC with respect to the IRS's reflection
coefficients. In addition, the derived update rules do not require the
re-evaluation of the joint probability density function of the observation or
its MGF. Most importantly, the proposed optimization algorithm is guaranteed
the global optimality. Finally, the numerical results are presented to show the
significant gain of the EC due to the IRS's assistance and the validity of the
derived special case of the EC.

inertial effects on electrons. In analogy to the classical Coriolis and
centrifugal forces, these effects are the spin-rotation coupling, the
centrifugal field coupling, the centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and the
centrifugal redshift. Depending on the phonon decay, these effects persist for
various picoseconds after excitation. Potential boosting of the effects would
make it a promising platform for vibration-based control of localized quantum
states and chemical reaction barriers.
  From a theoretical perspective, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the
time-dependent perturbative treatment of the rotating crystal lattice. We show
that the validity of the perturbative treatment is determined by the ratio of
the fine structure constant to the square of the phonon amplitude. This ratio
is of order unity for common rare-earth ions. We further provide a
semi-classical model capturing the strong-coupling limit and its connection to
the mechanical forces. The model explains the origin of the cut-off and why
multiple phonons are required to induce the effects.
  We show that the rotation can induce magnetic dipole transitions between
otherwise dark states. This might be of particular interest for the detection
of superconducting or magnetic impurities in semiconductors or insulators. In
addition, we propose that the centrifugal field coupling might be used to
control optical transitions between 2p orbitals.
  Finally, we show that the centrifugal redshift might be used to gain insight
into the local electron density. We demonstrate this by showing that the
quantitative agreement between simulation and semi-classical model can be used
to gain insight into the phonon frequency and the electron density in
ErBr$_3$ and to show that in YbF the centrifugal redshift can be used to
directly probe the character of the ground state.

efforts to design a novel framework for
building a generalizable, and robust intelligent driver assistance systems
(IDASs). First, we will introduce a novel framework for building a IDASs.
Second, we will show that this framework is able to produce a set of
performant systems, which can be used to build a robust IDAS. Finally, we will
show that our IDAS achieves a set of desired features including a high
performance, a low false positive rate, and a competitive cost compared to
the state-of-the-art systems.
  We argue that a IDAS is a system of several intelligent systems, and thus
we will use the system-of-systems (SoS) framework to design a IDAS. Using this
framework, we will define a set of requirements, including the functional,
performance, and social needs, for building a generalizable and robust IDAS.
These requirements will be used to evaluate any IDASs, and thus they are
crucial for the success of the SoS approach in designing a IDAS.
  To validate the proposed framework, we will use it to design a lane change
assistance system (LCAS). We will define a set of requirements for the LCAS,
and then use these requirements to design the system architecture, hardware,
and software. We will show that the resulting LCAS performs well in several
challenging scenarios, and thus it is a good example of a IDAS. Finally, we
will show that by using the proposed framework, we can build a LCAS, and thus
we believe that it can be used to design any IDAS.

designing a IDAS. The key to the success of this approach is to define a set
of clear requirements for the system. These requirements should include the
functional, performance, and social needs, and they should be used to design
and evaluate the IDAS. We have demonstrated that this approach can be used to
design a LCAS, and thus we believe that it can be applied to any IDAS.

change on knot diagrams. Any knot diagram
can be transformed into a trivial unknot diagram by a series of unknotting
operations plus some Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations have an important
role in knot theory; they are used to study the genus of knots, to construct
new invariants of knots, and to study the dynamics of knot diagrams. In this
paper, we study 4-letter unknotting operations, and we give a complete
classification of them.
  It is known that there are finite choices for unknotting operations. However,
the previous studies of unknotting operations are mainly ad-hoc. There is no
systematic way to classify all possible unknotting operations. This is
particulary true when we generalize unknotting operations to 4-letter operations
as we do in this paper. The main technical tool used in this classification is
a system of checks which an unknotting operation must satisfy. These checks
guarantee that an unknotting operation indeed produces an unknot after an
unknotting operation is applied to a knot diagram.
  We give a complete classification of all possible 4-letter unknotting
operations. We show that an unknotting operation must change the crossing type
of a knot diagram in a specific way. More precisely, an unknotting operation
must change a positive crossing to a negative crossing or vice versa. We give
a complete classification of all possible ways to change a crossing to an
unknotting operation.
  Unknotting operations are closely related to braid moves. It is interesting
to know if there is a connection between our 4-letter unknotting operations and
the classical braid group. We give some evidence that there is such a connection
between them.
  Finally, we give some open problems about unknotting operations. In particular,
we would like to generalize the system of checks that an unknotting operation
must satisfy to $n$-letter operations.
  The main purpose of this paper is to give a complete classification of
4-letter unknotting operations. However, along the way, we give some interesting
examples of local changes on knot diagrams. These local changes are not
unknotting operations. They are useful examples to illustrate some general
principles of changing a knot diagram to an unknot diagram.
  In Section \ref{sec:localchange}, we give some examples of local changes on
knot diagrams.

coordination by a team of strategic agents choosing to perform one of the two
actions each. We consider a repeated game of infinite horizon, where the
payoffs depend on the actions chosen by each pair of agents. Our goal is to
identify the conditions under which the team achieves a better payoff than the
one achieved by the agents acting non-cooperatively, i.e., playing a Nash
equilibrium. We apply tools from dynamical systems to construct a Lyapunov
function that measures the "distance" from the team to its best possible
cooperative outcome. We show that if the team is "dynamically stable," then
whatever trajectory of payoffs is achieved by the team is either non-improvable
or leads to a cooperative payoff within a distance of $1/r$ of the best possible
cooperative payoff, where $r$ is the discount factor of the agents. We also
show that the cooperative payoff achieved by the team is $r$-close to the
non-cooperative payoff if the Nash equilibrium is dynamically stable. These
results highlight the tradeoffs between the benefits of coordination and the
cost of deviating from the non-cooperative equilibrium.

physics in the future,
such as the Higgs and top quark measurements at the ILC/CLIC/ FCC-ee and the
LHC/WLCG, the need for improved fundamental constants measurements becomes
evident. The SI definition of the kilogram, which is based on the
equimolar mass of $^{238}$U and $^{nat}$Pt, will soon be replaced by the
definition based on the Avogadro constant. This new definition will open the
way to a complete set of seven fundamental physical constants definitions.
The definition of meter will be based on the speed of light, that of second
will be based on the caesium atom, that of kilogram will be based on the
Avogadro constant, that of ampere will be based on the elementary charge,
that of kelvin on the Boltzmann constant, that of mole on the Avogadro
constant and that of gram on the Planck constant. The knowledge of the
Planck constant is crucial for the definition of the meter, which will be
based on the speed of light. The knowledge of this constant is also important
for metrology in general and for the fundamental constants interrelations.
The Planck constant can be determined with high accuracy by several methods,
such as faraday's law of electrolysis, thermodynamic methods, mechanical
methods, Josephson junctions and ac methods. The results from all these methods
are now consistent with each other within their uncertainties, which are at
the level of $5 \times 10^{-8}$. The key challenge for the future is to
develop new techniques in order to break the $10^{-8}$ uncertainty barrier.
This will open the way to even more accurate fundamental constants
determinations and new applications in metrology, physics and technology.
This review paper presents the current knowledge and open issues in the
determination of the Planck constant and possible ways to further improve the
uncertainty of the measurement of this constant.
  In this paper, the determination of the Planck constant using different
methods is reviewed. The faraday law of electrolysis, thermodynamic methods,
mechanical methods, Josephson junctions and ac methods are presented. The
achievements and open issues of each method are discussed. The future
directions and possible new techniques in order to break the $10^{-8}$
uncertainty barrier are also presented.
  The determination of the Planck constant using different methods is
reviewed.

machine learning. The kernel choice and its related parameters tuning is one of
the main challenges in implementing kernel methods. Automatic Relevance
Determination (ARD) kernel allows the model to automatically choose the
dimensional features without any external information. However, the ARD kernel
incurs a high computational cost during training. Moreover, the kernel matrix
computation is not efficient for high-dimensional data. To address these
issues, we propose a novel dimensionality reduced ARD kernel, which uses the
principal component analysis (PCA) and incorporates the variance of the data
into the kernel function. The proposed method achieves a significant reduction
in training time and memory usage. Moreover, the kernel choice problem is
transformed into selecting the number of PCA components, which is more
intuitive and easier to tune. Experimental results on several classification
datasets show that our approach achieves comparable or better accuracy and
reduced training time compared to the state-of-the-art kernel methods.
Furthermore, the training time and the model size are significantly improved
when applying our approach to a real-world sentiment analysis problem.

annotations. We show that using easy annotations (i.e. annotations that are

multiple types of annotations (i.e. both text and point annotations) is
significantly better than using a single type of annotation.

systems are able to steer the entire beam towards a specific user-equipment
(UE), thus providing a spatially orthogonal channel. In this paper, we exploit
this property to design an interference-canceled (IC) nonorthogonal multiple
access (NOMA) system, referred to as spatial IC NOMA. In the spatial IC NOMA
system, the base station (BS) first uses its XL-MIMO capabilities to steer the
entire beam towards one of the UEs, thus eliminating the cross-link interference
for all the UEs. Then, the BS applies an IC operation to the observed signal to
recover the signals of all the UEs in a NOMA fashion. We derive the rate
performance of the proposed spatial IC NOMA system and compare it with that of
the conventional XL-MIMO based orthogonal multiple access (OMA) system and that
of an IC OMA system. It is observed that the proposed spatial IC NOMA system
outperforms both the XL-MIMO based OMA and the IC OMA systems in terms of rate
performance. Finally, we provide simulation results to verify the theoretical
observations and to investigate the gain that the proposed spatial IC NOMA
system can achieve in terms of rate compared to the conventional IC OMA system.
The simulation results show that the proposed spatial IC NOMA system can
achieve a significant rate gain of as high as $20$ bits per symbol (BPS) at a
moderate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of $10$ dB.

relax the training data constraint and learn a face alignment model in the

regularizes the general network with the indoor network by projecting similar

classification. DDAN is the first framework that uses multi-domain training to
perform face dense alignment in the wild. We validate our approach on the
AffWild2 and AffectMine databases, which include challenging samples with
occluded faces, and misaligned landmark annotations, respectively. Compared to
state-of-the-art methods, DDAN achieves superior performance in terms of
alignment error and robustness.

Alignment (UFA) Database, which includes 55,000 images with over 17 million

analogous to the Einstein's theory of gravitation, with a fractonic
generalization of the f(R) theories of gravity. The presence of fractons
provides a scenario where spatial translation and dilatation symmetry breaking
can be connected to the emergence of a gravitational-like behavior.

comprehensive picture of the fractonic behavior in these models. We also show
how nonlinear effects can lead to the creation of mobile fractons from an
immobile fracton state, and vice versa.

lack of edge modes, and how this can be used to classify fractonic phases.

theories, and for the interpretation of numerical results in particular.
Moreover, it provides a link between fractons and the more general class of

the relationship between academic
achievement and socio-emotional learning (SEL) in adolescents. Using a
representative sample of over 2,000 8th- and 10th-graders from the National
Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (AddHealth), I exploit the variation in
SEL skills across individuals and schools to estimate the causal effect of SEL
on academic achievement. I employ a difference-in-differences strategy that
controls for individual, family, peer, and school characteristics, as well as
time trends. My results show that adolescents with higher SEL skills tend to
have higher academic achievement, particularly in math. Specifically, a one
standard deviation increase in SEL is associated with a 4-6% increase in the
probability of scoring above the 75th percentile in reading and a 7-9% increase
in the probability of scoring above the 75th percentile in math. I also find
that the positive effect of SEL on academic achievement is stronger for
individuals from low-income and/or minority backgrounds. Finally, I find that
the positive effect of SEL on academic achievement persists even after
controlling for subsequent mental health and substance use behaviors in young
adulthood. Overall, this study provides strong evidence that SEL is an important
predictor of academic achievement in adolescence and has important policy
implications for investing in SEL programs, particularly for disadvantaged
youth.
  The appendix contains additional details on data sources, variables, and
estimation strategy. It also provides additional evidence on the validity of
the SEL measures and the robustness of the results to different specifications
and samples.

is a critical area used for the isolation of
infectious agents. The purpose of this study is to numerically investigate the
air leakage characteristics of an NPR with a deliberately induced negative
pressure and to evaluate the effectiveness of the room as an isolated space.
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is used to simulate the air leakage from the
NPR to the outside environment. The induced negative pressure in the NPR is
simulated by introducing a mass flow rate into the room as a sink term in the
governing equations. The pressure drop along the seal between the NPR and the
outside is simulated by introducing a pressure gradient term in the z-direction
along the seal surface. The air leakage from the NPR to the outside is
investigated by introducing a mass flow source (e.g., a ventilation system) on
the seal surface and by varying the pressure difference across the seal. The
air leakage characteristics are evaluated by varying the seal length, the
induced negative pressure in the NPR, and the pressure drop along the seal. The
results show that the negative pressure in the NPR can be maintained by
introducing a negative mass flow rate of up to 0.05 kg/s with or without the
pressure drop along the seal. The air leakage from the NPR to the outside can
be minimized by increasing the seal length. The seal length required to reduce
the air leakage to less than 0.1% of the ventilation rate is found to be in
the range of 1-10 m.
  This study demonstrates that the CFD can be used to evaluate the air
leakage characteristics of an NPR. The results can be used to design and
construct NPRs with minimal air leakage. Future studies can be conducted to
investigate the effectiveness of NPRs as isolated spaces by simulating the
transport of infectious agents from the NPR to the outside.

of flexibility in future low
carbon grids. However, the ability of storage to provide this service is
limited by its round trip efficiency. In this paper we present a new
efficiency metric for storage, the effective capacity, which takes into
account the efficiency and scheduling characteristics of storage. We then use
this metric to quantify the flexibility that storage can provide in a
residential energy system. We do this by solving a stochastic optimization
problem that minimizes the energy costs of a system consisting of a controllable
thermal energy storage (TES) and a flexible electricity supply profile. We
compare the effective capacity of the TES to that of a heat buffer, which is a
more traditional source of flexibility in residential systems. We show that the
effective capacity of the TES is significantly higher than that of the heat
buffer, and we investigate the impact of the price of electricity, the
round-trip efficiency of the TES, and the thermal energy available from the heat
buffer on the effective capacity of both.
  We find that the effective capacity of the TES is 2.5 times greater than that
of the heat buffer, and that the TES can reduce the standard deviation of
residential electricity costs by 35% compared to a system that uses only a
heat buffer. We also find that the effective capacity of the TES is reduced by
an efficiency loss of 10% per day, and that the benefit of the TES is
significantly greater when the price of electricity is high.
  We conclude that the effective capacity is a useful metric for quantifying
the flexibility of storage in energy systems, and that it can be used to
compare the benefits of different forms of storage.
  Finally, we note that the benefits of TES are likely to be greater in
non-residential systems, where the amount of thermal energy available is
likely to be greater.

resolves waves up to a wavenumber of 16. The parameter space is sampled using
a Latin Hypercube method. The resulting circulation regimes are classified
using a self-tuning clustering algorithm. The model reproduces several well
known circulation regimes, such as a modern Earth-like Hadley circulation and a
super-Earth scenario with a strong meridional heat transport. In addition, it
also produces circulation states that are not well represented by modern
observations, such as a multi-cell Hadley circulation with sea ice only at the
poles and a circulation with a strongly elevated tropopause.

produce a large number of different circulation regimes depending on the
strength of the radiative forcing and the strength of the atmospheric
friction. The resulting circulation states span a wide range of temperatures
and heat transports and are thus of particular interest for studies of
super-Earths and exoplanets with strong atmospheres.

circulation regimes that are not well separated in the parameter space. This
demonstrates that the algorithm is capable of capturing subtle differences in
the circulation patterns that are caused by small variations in the model

states that are separated by large barriers in the parameter space. This
demonstrates that the model is able to get stuck in local minima of the
atmospheric energy balance.

identify the most informative data
samples for human annotation, thereby improving the overall efficiency of
machine learning. However, in real-world scenarios, the data often comes from
multiple sources with varying sample costs. For instance, in an AL setting for
medical image classification, the images may be obtained from patients with
different disease severities. The images from more severe cases are likely to be
more difficult to obtain, and thus are of higher sample cost. The existing AL
strategies, however, do not differentiate between the costs of the samples.
This can lead to a suboptimal performance, as some high-cost samples are
dropped by the AL algorithms due to their uniform sampling nature. In this
paper, we propose a novel active learning algorithm that differentiates between
the data samples of varying costs. We formulate a mathematical optimization
problem that maximizes the expected reduction in the estimated test loss of a
new classifier over the previously trained ones, subject to a sample cost
budget constraint. We further develop an efficient algorithm to solve this
problem. We show through experiments that our approach significantly outperforms
the uniform sampling baseline and other non-uniform sampling algorithms in
scenarios where the data samples have varying costs.
  We also study the impact of the AL iterations on our algorithm. We observe
that at the early AL iterations, uniform sampling performs better than our
algorithm because the classifiers are not yet confident enough about the
samples. At the later iterations, however, our algorithm starts to significantly
outperform uniform sampling. We further observe that the performance gap
between our algorithm and uniform sampling gets larger as the number of AL
iterations increases. This is because our algorithm selects the samples with the
largest expected loss at the last iteration, which are likely to be the most
difficult, and thus are of higher sample costs. We also observe that the
performance gap between our algorithm and uniform sampling gets larger for
datasets with a larger proportion of high-cost samples. This is because our
algorithm starts to differentiate between the samples of varying costs more
significantly on such datasets.
  We study the impact of the number of samples to be queried at each AL
iteration on our algorithm. We observe that our algorithm performs the best when
a moderate number of samples are queried at each iteration. Querying too few
samples does not allow the classifier to learn significantly from the new
labeled samples, while querying too many samples may not be feasible in some
real-world settings.

number of desirable features for quantum computing. Further work will be
required to fully realise the potential of this centre and to develop it into

showed that such games admit $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria for
certain settings of $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. They left open, however, the
question of what settings of $(\epsilon,\lambda)$ are achievable. In this
work, we fundamentally extend their negative results to a much larger class of
strategic domains. Specifically, we show that there is a simple (but, as we
discuss, fundamentally complex) game in which players observe their own
actions, but get zero information about the actions of the other players. It
would still be tempting to think that such games would have many approximate

the professional knowledge
discovery for Information Systems (IS) PhD students is an unexplored topic.
While IS PhD students can benefit from Web search to discover and learn about
emerging topics in IS, the effectiveness of the search with and without
Web search personalisation remains unknown. This study investigates the impact
of Web search personalisation on the discovery of professional knowledge in
Web search for IS topics. We conducted two sets of experiments: (1) human
subject study with 10 participants to find out if the personalisation
algorithm used by Google Web search affects the discovery of professional
knowledge; and (2) an automatic study to find out if the Web search
personalisation algorithm affects the coverage of professional knowledge in
Web search. Our human subject study found that the personalisation algorithm
significantly affects the discovery of professional knowledge in Web search.
We found that 34% of search sessions that include professional knowledge
contain links to Wikipedia, and removing Wikipedia from search results
significantly reduces the coverage of professional knowledge in Web search.
Removing the personalisation algorithm increases the coverage by 18%. Our
automatic study found that removing the personalisation algorithm increases
the coverage of professional knowledge by Web search results by 5%. While
human subject study results are significantly higher than automatic study
results, automatic study results confirm that the Web search personalisation
algorithm affects the coverage of professional knowledge in Web search. We
conclude that the influence of Web search personalisation on the discovery of
professional knowledge for IS PhD students is significant and worthy of
further research.
  We contribute this study as PhD students are the future academics and
researchers who will teach and conduct research in IS and related fields.
Their knowledge discovery will influence their teaching and research. If
Web search personalisation influences the coverage of professional knowledge
for PhD students, then it will influence the body of knowledge in IS and
related fields. Further, the techniques developed in this study can be
extended to other fields of study.

such as Google, Bing, and Yahoo to improve their search algorithms to

physics beyond the Standard Model. Such a machine could provide a rich
programme of measurements, including: deep differential and differential
correlation measurements of new quark and lepton compositeness; studies of
small-x heavy quark and gluon production and the deep virtual Compton
scattering process; and searches for a Higgs dark sector vector boson and other
new physics signatures. In this paper, we report on the results of a
small-scale study of such an idea, including both a parametric study and a
more detailed study of a specific reference design that could achieve the
desired performance. The results of the study are presented in the form of
design requirements for a more detailed future study.

achieves luminosity of $\mathcal{L} = 10^{33}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, and has a
focus point lattice-based ring design with a long straight section to facilitate
a wide range of physics programmes. The study highlights the key components
required for the successful realisation of such a facility, including the
development of a high-energy muon source, a suitable main ring and possible
institute-wide programmes to leverage the physics and technology opportunities
available.

to drive a programme of heavy-quark hadron and hybrid physics via a fixed-target
programme. The study highlights the need for further detailed investigation of

a set of safe states by discretizing the control input space and using a
learning-based approach, thus allowing for the efficient computation of a
control barrier function. We prove that the proposed controller ensures the
invariance of the safe set, recovers from transient unsafe states, and satisfies
a worst-case safety guarantee. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach
through a safety-critical tracking problem, where the vehicle must track a
reference trajectory while avoiding static and dynamic obstacles.

transiently crossed safety boundaries and provides a worst-case safety guarantee
along the reference trajectory.

neutron scattering measurements at very low temperature. We show that the
normal core interaction is actually weaker than the Josephson coupling, but only
by a factor of order unity. We explain our results theoretically, and show that
our observations can be quantitatively accounted for by a simple balance between
the two couplings. Our work provides direct experimental evidence for the
competition between the normal core interaction and the Josephson coupling in a
real vortex liquid.

determines the value of the vortex-lattice spacing. Therefore, our observations
provide a quantitative explanation of recent experimental work on the
flux-line-lattice spacing in Nb.

the square of the London penetration depth, in agreement with recent theoretical
predictions. This proportionality provides a new method for determining the
spacing in liquid from measurements of the penetration depth.

Josephson coupling. This balance provides a direct test of the competition

a cylindrical solid particle
swimming by an oscillating wave-like actuation inside a Newtonian fluid under
low Reynolds numbers. We systematically vary the orientation of the particle
with respect to the oscillation direction to reveal the occurrence of
symmetry breaking and its consequences. We find that, depending on the
orientation, the particle shows either a direct motion in the drive direction
(symmetric motion) or a net motion in the transverse direction (asymmetric
motion). The asymmetric motion is observed in the form of a circular orbit,
a reciprocating motion in a straight line, and a combination of both. The
physical mechanism behind the asymmetric motion is the uneven distribution of
the drag force along the particle's surface due to the change in the flow
direction during the different phases of the drive cycle. This uneven
distribution results in an accumulation of the impulse imparted to the particle
in the direction of the asymmetric motion, which is responsible for the net
motion. We further show that the magnitude of the asymmetric motion increases
with increasing amplitude of the drive and increasing ratio of the particle
diameter to the wavelength of the oscillation. The presented results may be
useful in the design of microswimmers that are able to move in any direction of
interest by using anisotropic shapes and motion modes.
  From an engineering perspective, the problem studied here is of particular
interest since it shows that an anisotropic design is not necessary to
generate anisotropic swimming modes. A cylindrical particle with an
isotropic shape can be driven in an anisotropic way by an appropriately chosen
actuation scheme.
  The presented results may also be of interest in the context of
doppler-based chemical sensing, where the net motion is needed to create a
doppler shift on only one side of the particle.
  The results may further be useful in the design of microengines that are
able to move in any direction of interest.
  Finally, the results may be useful in the study of the dynamics of
biological cylinders such as sperm cells, where the direction of the
self-propelled motion is often different from the direction of the flagellar
wave.

$\gtrsim$500~pc from the centre. The ionised gas is embedded within, but does

scenes for training
deep neural networks that aim to learn to make decisions in a variety of
real-world scenarios. To this end, we present a novel end-to-end framework for
generating realistic traffic scenes, which combines the benefits of
semi-supervised learning and conditional generation. Our framework consists of a
two-stage conditional generation network that first generates the road layout
and then adds realistic traffic participants to the road to form a realistic
traffic scene. We demonstrate that our framework is capable of generating
realistic traffic scenes by comparing the traffic scenes it generates with
real-world traffic scenes. When trained with generated traffic scenes, our
deep neural network achieves a high degree of generalization, which is
demonstrated by the high accuracy it achieves when classifying traffic
participants in real-world traffic scenes.
  We also show that our framework can learn to generate traffic scenes that are
tailored to a specific task. For example, by incorporating a constraint that
removes the risk of right-turn collisions, our framework can be made to generate
traffic scenes that are safer for all road users. Such a constrained generation
is particularly important for autonomous vehicles, which must be able to make
decisions in a variety of real-world scenarios. Finally, we show that our
framework can be used to generate traffic scenes that are tailored to a
particular geographic region. For example, by incorporating a constraint that
removes the presence of streetlights, our framework can be made to generate
traffic scenes that are more representative of a particular developing country.
  In summary, our framework is capable of generating realistic traffic scenes
that can be used to train deep neural networks that are capable of making
decisions in a variety of real-world scenarios. The traffic scenes generated by
our framework are not only realistic but also tailored to a specific task,
which is important for autonomous vehicles.

methods for solving
time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) is the achievement of
accurate results at a reduced computational cost. In this work, we investigate
the performance of three different implementations of embedded Runge-Kutta (ERK)
schemes for stiff problems, with the aim of deriving time evolution operators
for solving the time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) equations. In
particular, we consider the classical fifth-order ERK scheme of Prince, a
fifth-order ERK scheme derived from a rational approximation of the exponential
map, and a tenth-order ERK scheme derived using the same rational approximation
method as that recently employed by Kryvashyts and Umansky to construct the
Shestakov-Sheplevitch-Tian (SST) solver. We show that all three schemes yield
identical time evolution operators when constructed using a rational
approximation of the exponential map, and thus have equivalent computational
costs. We further show that when constructed using a Taylor series approximation
of the exponential map, as in the Prince scheme, the three schemes have
different but fixed time costs, with the costs of the new schemes being
significantly better than that of the Prince scheme for large time steps. We
also show that fixed time costs can be achieved for the Taylor Prince scheme
through the use of a simple time step predictor-corrector strategy, and that
this scheme outperforms the new schemes when small time steps are required. We
conclude that the new schemes are preferable to the Taylor Prince scheme for
large time steps, and that further work is required to achieve optimal
performance in the TDDFT context.
  We also investigate the performance of these schemes in the context of
integrating a model Kohn-Sham equation, and show that the fifth-order schemes
have significantly better time costs than the tenth-order scheme for large time
steps. We further show that the SST solver outperforms the TDDFT schemes by
avoiding the need to solve a nonlinear equation, and that using a simple
iterative scheme to achieve self-consistency does not significantly impact the
time cost. Finally, we show that the time costs of the TDDFT and KS schemes can
be significantly improved through the use of a multistep scheme, and that this
approach may be of use in future work.

3D detection of pedestrian, which is a
challenging task due to the sparse and occluded nature of the targets in the
scene. The traditional 2D pedestrian detection methods suffer from boundary
extension errors and are unable to provide the critical information along the
Z-axis. On the other hand, 3D object detection methods provide the necessary
information but are expensive in terms of computational resources. To
effectively utilize the computational resources, detector training is performed
using a large batch size and multiple iterations of training are performed only
on a small validation set towards the end of the training. However, in a
production environment, the detector is deployed on a single batch basis and
must provide accurate detection on the entire test set. To effectively utilize
the computational resources during training and provide accurate detection on
the entire test set, we propose a novel 3D far-field pedestrian detection
method called \textit{FieldTracker}. The field in the method name represents
the 3D space in which we are interested in detecting the pedestrians. During
training, the method focuses on detecting the targets that are likely to be
present in the test set by learning a validation set specific density function.
To achieve this, the training process is supervised by a validation set
density estimation function learned from the labeled validation set. The
density estimation function is learned by first clustering the validation set
based on the 3D distance metric and then fitting a density function to the
cluster centers. The method learns the density function by minimizing the
Kluchner Sensitive Loss (KSL) between the probability distribution of the
validation set and the density function. The KSL is a novel loss function for
training detectors for far-field 3D object detection applications. To make the
validation set density estimation function applicable to the training set, the
density estimation function is normalized to the training set specific
probability distribution. The normalized density estimation function is used
for selecting the training set 3D rays (line-segments) on which the detector
is trained. The method selects the 3D rays by minimizing the KSL between the
probability distribution of the validation set and the normalized density
estimation function. The FieldTracker detector is trained on the selected 3D
rays. The FieldTracker method effectively utilizes the computational resources
during training and provides accurate detection on the entire test set
demonstrated by the experimental results.

in the navigation system of a
robotic snake. To achieve a high performance in this task, we present a new
snake registration system based on computer vision techniques. The system uses
two monocular cameras to detect the position of each rigid ring component and
then computes the global curve of the snake from these local information. To
detect the position of each ring, we employ a real-time object detection
approach based on the YOLOv3 computer vision algorithm. To further improve the
accuracy of this detection for our application, we augment the YOLOv3 model
using genetic algorithm to include information about the relative distance
between the ring components and the snake body orientation. Once the non-rigid
registration is achieved, we present and evaluate different methods to
compute the optimal body configuration that best fit the desired curve of
continuity.
  We present and evaluate the performance of three body configuration
optimization methods: (1) a genetic algorithm, (2) quasi-static with
model-based inverter controls, and (3) direct computation using a
look-up-table approach. We show that all three methods provide good results
however with different computational costs. The genetic algorithm is the most
flexible but the slowest, the look-up-table approach is the fastest but limited
to a specific snake configuration, and the inverter control method provides a
good trade-off between computational cost and generality.
  We also present and discuss a sensor error model that can be used to
post-process the results to avoid the snake from navigating too close to
obstacles. The model takes into account the circular nature of the sensor
errors, and it is computationally efficient.
  The presented work can be used to improve the navigation system of a
robotic snake by providing an accurate and computationally efficient
non-rigid registration method and different body configuration optimization
strategies. It can also be extended to other applications that require
flexible and computationally efficient computer vision and control strategies.
For example, it can be used to navigate a robotic snake in a mixed reality
environment where the real world visual features can be extended with virtual
ones.

dynamic scene. We present a new approach that estimates scene flow from
high-resolution stereo video. Our approach uses a fully convolutional network
(FCN) to estimate point cloud features and motion vectors. The network is
trained on individual frames of the video sequence, rather than pairs of
frames. This allows the network to exploit the information present in an
entire frame, rather than just matching points between two frames. We show
that this results in a significant improvement in scene flow estimation. We
also show that by operating on the output of a stereo matching network, we can
improve the scene flow estimation by incorporating disparity information. We
present a new benchmark for scene flow estimation from video sequences. The
benchmark includes a new dataset containing high-resolution stereo video
sequences of dynamic scenes as well as a dataset created from the KITTI dataset.
We also present a novel evaluation metric that captures the temporal
consistency of the estimated motion vectors.

control over a quantum walker. Specifically, we show that a single photon can
selectively trap or eject a quantum of an entangled-photon pair from a
quantum walk. This is achieved by interfering it with the walk in such a way to
produce a specific entanglement-dependent overlap. Moreover, our scheme allows
the trapped quanta to be transferred to another walk in a different direction,
demonstrating non-classical signal transmission. Finally, we show that the
quanta can be used to drive another quantum walk, effectively acting as a
"quantum catalyst." The proposed technique provides an unprecedented level of
control over an otherwise unmanipulated quanta, opening the door to a variety
of applications, including quantum computation and communication.

entangled-photon pair at the walk's vertices. The KD coin is a Suzukii-type
coin that, unlike most of the well-studied coin, produces an entangled pair of
photons. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time the KD rules are
implemented to generate an entangled pair of photons. We show that the
resulting walk is maximally entangled and can be used to achieve an unprecedented
level of control over the quantum of an entangled pair. The proposed technique

drive other quantum walks, effectively acting as a "quantum catalyst."

species competition under the framework developed here.

extinct in the presence of an asymmetric immigration rate. Surprisingly, the
species that is more resistant to displacement by the other can still go extinct
if it is the one that is less able to recolonize areas occupied by the other.
These extinction results are explained in terms of the creation of "islands of
invasion" that can lead to long-lived coexistence in a parameter region that
would otherwise lead to competitive exclusion.

opportunities for correcting aberrations in electron microscopes. Here, we
present a numerical approach to optimize such a phase plate for any given
specimen tilt and orientation with respect to the deflection system's
symmetry-axes. For this, the dynamical transmission function of the projector
part of the microscope is calculated for a square grid of tilt orientations and
combined to construct a look-up table. For an arbitrary specimen orientation,
the corresponding tilt orientation with minimal aberrations is then interpolated
from this table. The look-up table was measured and its accuracy was found to
be better than 1 mrad for tilt orientations between -10$^{\circ}$ and
+10$^{\circ}$. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by optimizing a
phase plate for a negatively stained tobacco mosaic virus aggregate and show
that this leads to a significant improvement of the structure factor
reconstruction, in particular for large tilt angles.

from the corresponding defocus map measured with an unoptimized phase plate.
This is shown for a negatively stained red blood cell and an image of
interconnected holes. For some orientations, structure analysis reveals that
the phase plate can optimize not only the tilt but also the image magnification
and rotation. This is due to the fact that the specimen's image becomes
periodic for these orientations and thus shares some symmetry-axes with the
phase plate.
  Our approach is generally applicable to all types of transmission electron
microscopes and can be particularly useful for microscopes that are not
equipped with a phase plate, such as those using differential phase contrast

contextual information of the dialogue at every time step. However, the
attention mechanism in the encoder of the existing sequence-to-sequence
architectures, which is used to weigh the relevance of each utterance, is
static and is not able to dynamically adjust according to the task at hand
depending on the context. For example, for the dialogue about the restaurant
reservation, the attention should be first put on the utterance that mentioned
the reservation, and then on the utterances that mentioned the available time
and the preferred cuisine. To this end, we propose a novel contextual
encoder, namely Dynamic Contextual Encoder (DCE), which dynamically adjusts
the order of the utterances to be encoded based on the contextual information
contained in each utterance. The order is further reinforced by the decoder
during training, resulting in a reinforced dynamic order. Our experimental
results show that the DCE outperforms the state-of-the-art contextual encoders
and also results in a significant reduction in the number of times the model
needs to look back in the dialogue to predict the next utterance.
  Furthermore, our experiments show that the model is able to learn task-specific
representations of the utterances, resulting in a significant improvement in
the task-conditional generalization.
  We also observe that the model is able to learn a task-specific dictionary
where the key is the utterance and the value is the concept that the utterance
represents, and use this observation to propose a method to evaluate the
expressiveness of a dataset from the perspective of the encoder.
  Finally, our observation that the task-conditional generalization is
significantly improved by the task-specific representations, motivates our
analysis of the effect of the number of tasks on the generalization, and shows
how the existing multi-task learning datasets are too rich to learn task
distinct representations, and how our dataset is designed to learn such
representations.

dialogue understanding and generation tasks, and also hopes to spur further

  We propose to use a registration based approach to detect loop. The approach
first registers two point clouds and calculates the registration error. If the
registration error exceeds a certain threshold, it means that the two point
clouds are from two far apart places, i.e., a loop. To make the loop detection
robust, we propose to scale the point cloud before registration. The scaling
makes the system robust to different vehicle speeds.
  To make the system efficient, we turn off the loop detection when the vehicle
is moving by a certain speed. The reason is that the vehicle speed and the
vehicle acceleration can provide a lot of information about the driving scene
and whether a loop is likely to be detected. If the vehicle speed is higher
than a certain threshold, we turn off the loop detection for a certain period
of time, e.g., 10 seconds after the loop detection is last triggered. This is
because the vehicle speed is likely to be even higher in the next few seconds,
and a loop is less likely to be missed.
  The whole system is implemented and tested on an autonomous vehicle platform.

which is higher than 1 KHz, and achieve very good performance. The system can
detect all the loops in a 1.5 Km long test track with an accuracy of 99%. It
can also run in a real city test track and detect all the loops with an accuracy

  We present a new framework for the automatic generation of high-quality,
human-readable comments for R(ruby) methods. Our approach relies on statistical
models that guess the semantic categories that the authors of the methods
intended to express and then chooses the most suitable text from a corpus of
existing comments in the same category. We show that this approach outperforms
previous comment generation techniques both in terms of accuracy and in terms

human-readable comments for R(ruby) methods. Our approach relies on statistical
models that guess the semantic categories that the authors of the methods
intended to express and then chooses the most suitable text from a corpus of
existing comments in the same category. We show that this approach outperforms
previous comment generation techniques both in terms of accuracy and in terms

graphene sheets are described by a
massless Dirac fermion Hamiltonian. We show that in spatially inhomogeneous
polarization fields, the electron energy spectrum is given by a generalized
Dirac equation. This is achieved by mapping the electron problem to an
equivalent problem of flat bands in a graphene bilayer coupled to spatially
varying magnetic fields in the Landau gauge. We also show that the generalized
Dirac equation can be obtained directly by using the Weyl representation of
the imaginary-time fermionic operators and by linearizing the graphene
Hamiltonian around the saddle point solution that describes the ground state.
Both approaches allow us to explicitly show that in the absence of polarization
fields, the spectrum reduces to the massless Dirac equation. Furthermore, we
show that spatially inhomogeneous polarization fields lead to spatially
varying long-range electric fields that couple to the electrons through the
piezoelectric term in the graphene Hamiltonian. These coupling are responsible
for the electron energy spectrum described by the generalized Dirac equation.
The electron density is also calculated and it is shown that it is determined
by the spatial inhomogeneity of the polarization field. Finally, we show that
the generalized Dirac equation can be used to study the quantum Hall phases of
graphene. Specifically, we calculate the quantum Hall conductivity using the
generalized Dirac equation and show that it agrees with previous results
obtained by using the Weyl fermion representation of the time-dependent
Hamiltonian.

of soliton solutions for the $\mathbf{U}(2)$-invariant Gross-Pitaevski equation
(GPE), derived within two-component Bose-Einstein condensation model, which
features a repulsive cubic self-interaction and an attractive logarithmic
interaction between the two components. The case, when such a GPE model is
coupled to an external harmonic trap, is also considered. Within the
two-component generalised mean-field model under consideration we investigate
fully the situation when one of the components supports a ground state soliton
while the second component has an excess of the condensation, which leads to a
fragment of the soliton, attached to it as a bound state, soliton fragment or
quasiparticle. We show that this situation occurs, provided the ratio between
the strengths of single-body, logarithmic intercomponent, and intercomponent
effective coupling constants exceeds a certain threshold. We also show that in
this case the soliton and the quasiparticle are both spectrally and orbitally
stable if the threshold is reached in a certain range of values, and that an
instability occurs if the threshold is reached in an another certain range of
values. In the cases of soliton and quasiparticle an explicit characterization
of the thresholds is performed, while for the bound state attached to the
quasiparticle or fragment (which is also a quasiparticle) this is not possible
due to its highly excited character.
  From the mathematical point of view, the given problem consists in the
nonlocal, semi-linear parabolic equation with a symmetry constraint. To solve
it, we use a symmetry-based approach, which is reduced to a planar Hamiltonian
system, and then to a set of two coupled, nonlocal, semi-linear elliptic
equations with algebraic constraints. These constraints ensure that the
searched-for condensation profiles possess the $\mathbf{U}(2)$-symmetry. The
stability analysis is based on the linearization of the given Hamiltonian
system (or equivalently, of the coupled nonlocal, semi-linear elliptic
equations) at the soliton solution, and on the determination of the signs of
the eigenvalues of the corresponding linearization operator. The existence of
a threshold of the intercomponent coupling necessary for the soliton stability
is found to be connected with a bifurcation of the Hamiltonian system
equations.

system, it can also be exploited by pathogens to hijack and navigate the

pathway exploited by the rabies virus allows it to navigate the nervous system
with precision and target specific neuronal populations for replication. Here,
we use a machine learning approach to uncover the molecular determinants of
neuronal infectivity. We find that the infectivity of a neuron is largely
determined by its layer of origin, with deeper layers being more resistant to
infection. We further show that this resistance is reflected in the
connectome-based proximity of neurons to their point of origin, with deeper
neurons being less likely to be in close apposition to the virus-laden axon. In
addition, we find that the infectivity of a neuron is also determined by its
morphological features, with neurons that are more fusiform in shape being more
easily infected. Finally, we find that the relationship between neuronal
morphology and infectivity is largely independent of layer, suggesting that
multiple factors contribute to the ability of viruses to navigate and target
specific neuronal populations.

infectivity of a neuron based on its morphological features and layer of origin.

navigate and target specific neuronal populations.

in uncovering the complex rules that govern the behavior of pathogens in the
nervous system.

features of the neurons that comprise the nervous system, and that the
relationship between neuronal morphology and pathogen behavior can be used to
