vertical axis, i.e., the direction of gravity. This results in panoramas in
the form of cylindrical or spherical images. In this paper, we propose a
novel approach to create horizontal panoramas by moving in circular motion
while capturing horizontal strips. The main advantage of horizontal panoramas
over cylindrical or spherical ones is that they provide a square field of view
while eliminating the perspective distortions. This is particularly useful in
modern days when most of the people use square or close-to-square displays to
view the panoramas. To create the horizontal panoramas, first, the camera
orientation and position need to be estimated. To this end, we exploit the
reflective tape markers attached to the moving base of the camera to provide
range information from one frame to the next. Then, using structure from motion
techniques, we estimate the camera trajectory and recover the horizontal
panorama by rectifying the images along the horizontal axis. Our system is
implemented using a custom-built rig moving in a circular path and is tested
under various conditions including both indoor and outdoor environments as well
as different resolutions and lens focal lengths.
  We believe that the main contribution of this work is to show the feasibility
of creating horizontal ground plane panoramas. This is achieved by moving in
circular motion while capturing horizontal strips. The proposed system is
implemented using an affordable setup and provides a novel application in the
field of panoramic imaging.

STIS absorption-line spectra. We analyze the ionization state, column
density, and kinematics of the ionized gas, and compare the properties of
these galaxies to more than 50 $z\sim2$ galaxies with unresolved ionized gas
spectra. The resolved galaxies have on average higher ionization parameters
than the unresolved sample, and their ionization parameters correlate strongly
with stellar mass. The resolved galaxies also have higher gas column densities
than the unresolved galaxies, and the gas densities correlate strongly with
stellar mass as well. These results suggest that the ionized gas in more
massive $z\sim2$ galaxies is more tightly wrapped around the stars. We do not
see a correlation between dynamical mass (or velocity dispersion) and
ionization parameter, which suggests that the gas in $z\sim2$ galaxies is not
merely responding to the stellar radiation field, but rather to the total
luminosity (or star formation rate). Finally, we find that the ionization
parameters of the galaxies in our sample are an order of magnitude lower than
that of giant elliptical galaxies in the local universe. This suggests that
the ionization state of the ionized gas evolves strongly with galaxy mass,
consistent with the idea that the gas in $z\sim2$ galaxies is more tightly
wrapped around the stars.

systems. This paper aims to investigate the relationship between weather
conditions and the performance of air transportation systems. The performance
metrics used are the on-time performance and the cancellations of flights. The
relationship investigation is conducted by calculating the average delay and
the cancellation rate for each weather condition code. The results show that
weather conditions do impact the performance of air transportation. Furthermore,
the average delay and the cancellation rate for each weather condition code are
calculated. The highest average delay and the highest cancellation rate are
obtained for weather condition code 6 and weather condition code 3, respectively.
It is also found that the top five weather conditions that cause the most
delays are heavy snow, heavy rain, freezing rain, thunderstorms, and blowing
snow. The top three weather conditions that cause the most cancellations are
heavy snow, blowing snow, and thunderstorms. The findings of this paper can be
used as a reference for the improvement of air transportation systems as well as
the planning of the activities of all stakeholders involved in this sector.
Further research can be conducted by investigating the relationship between
weather conditions and other performance metrics of air transportation, such as
passenger and cargo volume, as well as the revenue and cost of the industry.
Additionally, the effects of the weather conditions on the air transportation
system can be analyzed by looking at the micro-level, i.e., the individual
aircraft, and not only at the macro-level, i.e., the entire air transportation
system.

underwater acoustic (UAQ) equalization. However, it suffers from the
oversmoothing problem, especially at the beginning of the iteration process.
This paper proposes a novel DPRNN-based equalization method, called
iterative conditional DPRNN (ICDPRNN), to mitigate the oversmoothing. In the
iterative equalization process, the DPRNN is used to model the conditional
probability density function (PDF) of the channel, and the conditional
expectation (CE) is used to equalize the signal. However, the DPRNN should be
trained to keep a certain degree of uncertainty to cover the conditional PDF,
and the CE should not be used to update the DPRNN in each iteration. The
optimization objective function includes not only the equalization performance
measure, such as the mean square error (MSE), but also an entropy term to
guarantee the uncertainty of the DPRNN. The ICDPRNN has been evaluated using
two typical underwater communication (UWC) datasets. The simulation results
show that the ICDPRNN outperforms the traditional DPRNN and other state-of-the-
art methods, such as the iterative Kalman RNN (IKRNN), in terms of equalization
performance and model uncertainty.

public emotions towards events in the world. However, there are also
cyberbullying and hate speech that are spread through social media. The
spreading of hate speech can lead to the spread of hatred and violence, as
well as the erosion of public order. Therefore, the sentiment analysis task
can be used to detect and remove hate speech from social media. However, this
task is difficult because of the high cost of labeling data. To overcome this
problem, we propose a new method for detecting hate speech by projecting a
high-dimensional feature space to a low-dimensional space using t-SNE and

accuracy of 68.3%.

require human-annotated data. Our approach uses a statistical language model
to score the sentiment of social media posts and then uses a threshold to
determine whether the post is hate speech or not. The threshold is trained on
unlabeled data using a small set of labeled examples. We use a small set of
labeled examples to train a classifier for each language and then use the
unlabeled data to calibrate the classifiers. The models are trained for 20
different languages using 5,000 minutes of Twitter text. We show that the
models can be used to classify hate speech in 20 different languages with an
accuracy of 73%.

However, pesticide use is
increasingly linked to environmental problems and health risks. To minimize
these negative effects, it is essential to understand the factors that
determine the adoption of integrated pest management (IPM). This study
investigates the factors that influence the adoption of IPM among farmers in
Benin. A random sample of 400 farmers was selected for the study. The
appropriate method of estimating the probability of adopting a technology as
large as the IPM is the logistic regression. The results show that the
probability of adopting the IPM increases with the level of education,
experience, access to credit, membership of a farmers group, the level of
information on IPM and the number of extension visits. The results also show
that the probability of adopting IPM decreases with the level of income,
distance to the market and the level of pesticide use. The study concludes
that the main factors that determine the adoption of IPM in Benin are
education, experience, access to credit, information on IPM, income, distance
to the market and the level of pesticide use. The study recommends that
government and non-governmental organizations should increase support to
farmer groups in order to increase the adoption of IPM in Benin.

matrix. Here we consider the case when the sparse matrix is represented by its
adjacency matrix, specifically when this matrix is bidiagonal. In this case,
using algebraic and number theoretic properties of the adjacency matrix, we
manage to find a relatively simple expression for the inverse of the adjacency
matrix.
  In particular, for the tridiagonal adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph, e
.g. a tree or a cube, we derive a simple expression for the inverse in a form
which explicitly shows the sparse structure of the inverse. For a tree, this
expression is such that the support of the entries of the inverse is exactly
the same as the support of the original sparse matrix, plus a small number of
additional vertices. For the cube, the support of the entries of the inverse
covers exactly half of the vertices of the cube, plus three additional ones.

adjacency matrix of a cube currently is not well understood.

known in order to determine all other entries of the inverse is bounded by the
number of its nonzero diagonal entries.

construct a fast algorithm for calculating the inverse of a given (potentially
different) sparse matrix, by "transplanting" the relevant entries of the
inverse of the particular bidiagonal matrix considered here.

cardinality. In this work we consider the SGP for the class of chordal graphs.
We show that finding a minimum strong geodetic set in a chordal graph is
NP-complete. We also show that, in contrast with the general case, for the
class of interval graphs a minimum strong geodetic set can be found in
polynomial time.
  We also study the parameterized complexity of the problem with respect to
the geodetic number~${\beta}(G)$. We show that, for general graphs, the problem
is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to~${\beta}(G)$. Moreover, for the
class of chordal graphs, we give an algorithm that, given an instance~$(G,S)$
and a geodetic set~$S$ of size~$k$, determines whether~$S$ is strong geodetic
and, if so, finds a minimum strong geodetic set of size at most~k+1. Finally,
we observe that, for the consideration of this latter result, an alternative
formulation of the problem, which we call the Restricted Strong Geodetic
Problem (RSGP), is useful.
  Both the NP-completeness result and the exact algorithm for interval graphs
extend to the RSGP. However, for the fixed-parameter tractability of the RSGP
for general graphs we cannot establish the same parameterization as for the
SGP.
  All the results for the RSGP have interesting consequences for finding
minimum strong geodetic sets. In particular, for the class of chordal graphs,
we show that, given a minimum strong geodetic set~S, it is possible to find a
minimum strong geodetic set of the same cardinality as~S, or a geodetic set
of size at most~|S|+1.

graphs, a minimum strong geodetic set can be found in polynomial time.

in empathetic dialogue are limited in their ability to recognize affect in

introduce AudioPy, an open-source Python library for affective audio
classification that integrates multiple audio feature extractors and machine
learning models to recognize emotions in audio while remaining self-contained
and efficient. AudioPy provides a simple API for easy integration into
applications and services, and it can be used as a building block for
developing a variety of applications, including speech recognition systems,
natural language processing toolkits, and virtual avatars that can engage in
realistic and empathetic dialogue with people.
  AudioPy is composed of three main components: AudioDataLoader, ModelHub,
and PyCore. AudioDataLoader is a library of data loaders that integrates
multiple open-source and commercial audio feature extraction tools, including
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Mozilla DeepSpeech, Vosk, and Kaldi. These data
loaders wrap these external services in a way that makes them easy to use and
coordinate from Python. ModelHub is a library of machine learning models
that integrates AudioDataLoader's features with a variety of open-source
machine learning models, including scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch.
ModelHub makes it easy to use these models in an ensemble with
user-configurable weights and thresholds. PyCore is the core of AudioPy and
provides a simple API for easily using AudioPy in applications. PyCore
provides a simple Python API that makes it easy to use AudioPy's features,
including data loaders, model hub, and a core, all in one place. PyCore is
the main entry point for using AudioPy in applications.

example, it can run simultaneously with the Mozilla DeepSpeech model to
improve its emotion recognition performance. AudioPy is also highly scalable
and can run on large distributed computing systems to take advantage of

magnetic remanence and coercivity as a function of temperature. At 300 K, the
films exhibit a high coercivity of 0.14 T and remanence of 0.35 remanent magnetization
at saturation. Upon cooling to 2 K, the coercivity decreases to 0.04 T with
remanence increasing to 0.65 remanence at saturation. The temperature
dependence of the coercivity and remanence is consistent with a spin glass
transition at Tg = 60 K.

simulate the experimental results. The model consists of AFI and BFI sublattices
with random exchange interactions between the spins. The magnetic properties of
the model are probed by performing Monte Carlo simulations to obtain the
equilibrium remanence and coercivity as a function of temperature. We find that
by tuning the exchange interactions in the model, we can obtain good agreement
with the experimental results provided that a strong anisotropy term is
included. We find that the origin of the anisotropy is the difference in the
atomic size between Mn and Ga.

results provides a pathway to understanding the origin of the spin glass
transition in MnGa. We find that the anisotropy in the exchange interactions
arising from the difference in atomic size between Mn and Ga is the key to
understanding the magnetic properties of this material.

of spin glass transition temperatures. This provides a pathway to designing
new materials with tailored spin glass transition temperatures.

of such hybrid methods to global minimizers hinges on the discretization error
induced by restricting the discrete global optimization to the graph, with
corresponding implications on the stepsize control in the local minimization.
This work aims at deriving a priori and random boundedness results on
discretization errors for general spatial graphs, with a particular focus on
those relevant to optimal transport problems. We prove that, under mild
assumptions on the graph connectivity and on the cost functions, there exist
non-negative bounds on the discretization errors that are both a priori (i.e.,
dependent on the geometry of the domain and the cost functions) and random
(specifically, they include bounds on the expected value and higher moments of
the discretization error for a given geometry/domain).
  We derive these results by combining graph theoretical arguments with
functional inequalities such as the quadratic form lemma and results on
Poincare inequalities. The results are illustrated on several examples,
including costs involving polynomial distances and unitary costs (as in the
Monge-Ampere equation). Finally, we provide a numerical example showing the
practical implications of the derived bounds in an optimal transport
application.

shortest paths, connectivity.

early-type galaxies (ETGs). Utilizing the imaging data from the Hubble Space
Telescope (HST), we measure the surface brightness profiles and examine the
properties of the tidal features (such as the flux, radius, and contrast
contrast) for a sample of 21 massive ETGs. We find that about 55% of these
galaxies have detectable tidal features. The occurrence of tidal features is
more common in galaxies with higher stellar mass, bulge-to-total ratio, and
central black hole mass. The properties of tidal features (such as flux and
contrast) are more similar to the galaxy nuclei. The existence of these tidal
features suggests that the sample galaxies are in or have recently experienced
major mergers. The lack of or weak tidal features in some galaxies indicates
that internal dissipation or the so-called "galactic fountain" may have
efficiently destroyed the tidal structures. The occurrence of mergers among
ETGs is consistent with the merger-driven evolution scenario proposed by
Toomre (1977) and his collaborators. The detailed properties of tidal features
will be reported in a companion paper and will be used to constrain the models
of galaxy mergers.

scans ("Emittance Scans") was
introduced at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in 2015. The scans were
performed systematically in every fill with the full-beam luminosity of
ATLAS. They were used for monitoring the luminosity with high statistical
accuracy and for training the start-of-fill luminosity monitoring algorithms
with in-real-time data. The scans consisted of a slow oscillation of the beam
emittances combined with a fast oscillation of the closed orbit, which was
measured by a large number of interferometer systems placed along the entire
LHC ring. The use of the fast oscillation allowed for a large increase in the
statistical accuracy of the results due to the improved signal-to-noise ratio
and a reduction in the scan time by a factor of 100. The improved
reproducibility of the results and the large number of events allowed for a
highly precise measurement of the beam-to-beam interferometer systems
("beam striptool" measurement) and a measurement of the not yet commissioned
long-range muon interferometry systems. The scans also allowed for the
measurement of the beam-beam compensation (BBC) kick strengths, which agreed
very well with the values obtained from the individual tune measurements and
with the values required for the operation with the high luminosity lenses.
Several changes to the LHC beam parameters and several different fast
oscillation modes were tested during the scans, showing the robustness of the
method. The experience gained with the LHC "Emittance Scans" will be used for
the development of new scan modes and systems for the future high-luminosity
LHC.
  In this paper a general description of the "Emittance Scan" system is
given, followed by a detailed discussion of the measurement principles,
including the measurement of the fast oscillation with the interferometer
systems, the beam-to-beam interferometer systems ("beam striptool")
measurement, the measurement of the BBC kick strengths, and the possible
measurement of a muon spectrum. The experience gained from the commissioning,
operational use and offline analysis is discussed, including the
characterization of the LHC "kick" and several possible applications such as
the measurement of a beam-beam compensation system and a proton bunch
separation using a muon interferometer. Finally the advantages and
disadvantages of the system are discussed and possible future applications
and extensions are presented.

footprints. We find that a large number of MLMs (about 40%) have been
identified as pyramid schemes, and that many of these (about 70%) are still
operating today. We also find that pyramid schemes often disguise themselves
as MLMs by adopting MLM business models and registering themselves as
corporations. We find that they do so in response to pressure from law
enforcement and regulators. Finally, we find that both MLMs and pyramid schemes
often use get-rich-quick schemes as a recruitment strategy, which puts their
participants at risk of financial harm.

and the threat of pyramid schemes to its participants.

industries that are vulnerable to scams and scheme activity.

improve the experience of people looking to start a side hustle or join a
business online.

Neural Networks (CNN) and Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been successfully used for time-series analysis
and signal processing. However, these models are known to be computationally
expensive and difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices. In this
paper, we propose a novel architecture called DeepFog, which combines
LSTM/CNN with the fog computing paradigm to overcome the limitations of
deep-learning models. DeepFog consists of a local model (L-model) and an
aggregated model (A-model). The L-model is deployed on the edge device to
process a portion of the input data and returns a partial output to the
aggregated model. The A-model is deployed on the fog node to process the
remaining input data and combine the partial output with its own output to
generate the final output. We have implemented a proof-of-concept of DeepFog
using Python and evaluated its performance using a CNN model and a
weather-forecasting dataset. Experimental results show that DeepFog reduces
the computation latency by $42\%$ and energy consumption by $31\%$ compared to
a traditional deep-learning model.

present a novel approach to the problem by modelling the Galactic context of
microbial evolution on Earth. If life on Earth originated from endogenous
chemical reactions, we should see evidence of a temporal gap between the
emergence of life's building blocks and the origin of life itself. Conversely,
if life originated from cometary or meteoritic material, the timescale should
be shorter. To investigate this, we calculated the timescales for the formation

QED. The concept of quantum duality for non-Abelian gauge theories was recently
established in terms of two-color QCD, where the vector gluons are replaced by
vector photons of helicities $\pm 1$. The idea behind the proposed model is
based on the fact that in nature we have two-component vector bosons: gluons
and photons. While photons interact only with charged fermions and vector
bosons, the gluons in addition to charged fermions interact also with each
other. It is natural to ask what a theory in which photons interact with each
other in the same way as gluons, but with only charged fermions would look
like? The proposed model of quantum duality for QED is an attempt to
mathematically regularize this question.
  The paper shows that the proposed model of quantum duality for QED can be
obtained by making a suitable substitution between the electromagnetic and
Faddeev-Popov ghosts fields in the QED effective action. The resulting model
is found to be given by a sum of two QED-like effective actions, one for
helicity $\pm 1$ photons and a (imaginary) two-color QCD-like effective action
for the "gluons". The total charge of the photons is screened due to their
interaction with the "gluons". The model has a natural application to the
quantum theory of the electromagnetic field where the "gluons" are to be
identified with the condensate of the virtual quarks.
  The paper presents an analytical and perturbative study of the proposed
model. It is established that the model is free from ghosts and it has a
physical ground state. The effective charge of the proposed model is
calculated and it is found to have the same asymptotic properties as the QCD
coupling constant. The light-cone like effective Lagrangian of the proposed
model is obtained and it shows that the electromagnetic field interacts with a
cloud of "gluons". The energy density of the electromagnetic field is
calculated and it is found to have a screening behavior.
  In the strong coupling limit, the proposed model has an analogy to the
Wigner-Weyl symmetry where the electromagnetic field interacts with a cloud of
quark-antiquark condensates.

local situation. Under this architecture, the commander must be able to
autonomously update the mission plan in real time based solely on vehicle
reports. We describe three algorithms developed for this purpose: a
graph-based algorithm that is guaranteed to find the optimal plan in time on
board a typical unmanned aerial system, a genetic algorithm that is capable of

dynamically changing graph, particularly under the framework of a sliding

networked system, such as a wireless sensor network or a social network, where
the status of the system changes over time. In this context, maintaining the
accuracy of the node count near the true count near all times is crucial. To
induce efficiency in the count update process, we utilize a distributed
inference mechanism where the nodes of the graph (or the system) provide
information to the counting module in the form of a local signal, and the
module updates the count based on the aggregate of the local signals. We
consider two types of local signals: a binary signal and a Gaussian signal. We
show that the proposed binary signal based scheme, which uses majority voting
between the local and global signals, achieves a sublinear time complexity of
$\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ with a bounded error of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$, where
$n$ is the number of nodes. We also show that the Gaussian signal based scheme
achieves a higher accuracy with an error bound of $\mathcal{O}(1/n)$. We
furthermore show that our scheme is robust to node failures and new node
inclusions. We also show that our scheme is energy efficient as it requires
each node to send a small amount of information to the counting module over a
sliding window of $k$ time units, where $k$ is typically small, e.g.,
$\mathcal{O}(10^3)$.

paper presents a novel framework for traffic state estimation using geosensor

traffic states. Finally, the estimated traffic states are validated using
traditional methods that use traffic sensors. The proposed framework is
applied to estimate the traffic states on a part of the I-405 freeway in

states with a high degree of accuracy.

traffic states. This paper presents such a framework. It identifies geosensors
and estimates traffic states and evaluates the effectiveness of the framework

anomalous Nernst effect in the magnetically ordered state of the candidate
topological semimetal candidate Cu$_2$OSEs (E = S, Se). From a theoretical
perspective, the origin of such a large anomalous Nernst coefficient in
magnetic topological materials is not fully understood and requires further
investigation. In particular, the role of the spin degree of freedom and
magnetic scattering is not well understood. To this end, we have performed
first-principle calculations of the anomalous Nernst coefficient in
Cu$_2$OSeTe and Cu$_2$OSse crystals. We find that the large anomalous Nernst
coefficient in this material can be explained by considering the sum of two
contributions: one related to the spatial variation of the spin accumulation
along the temperature gradient and the other related to the magnetic scattering
of electrons. Our results provide a theoretical explanation of the
experimental findings and highlight the importance of the magnetic scattering
term in this material.
  We also investigate the effect of applying a hydrostatic pressure on the
anomalous Nernst coefficient in this material, finding that it increases with
pressure. To explain this finding, we analyze the evolution of the electronic
and magnetic structure under pressure. We find that the exchange splitting of
the bands, the carrier concentration, and the strength of the magnetic
scattering decrease with pressure, which contributes to the increase of the
anomalous Nernst coefficient. Our results provide a theoretical framework to
investigate the effect of pressure on the anomalous Nernst coefficient in
related materials.

Cu$_2$OSeTe, finding that it is large at temperatures close to the magnetic
transition temperature. This finding opens the door to the design of
thermoelectric devices that exploit the anomalous Nernst effect in
topological materials.

investigate the effect of pressure on the anomalous Nernst coefficient in
related materials and provide a theoretical framework to design materials with
large anomalous Nernst coefficient.

people in society, and ask whether individual differences in the structure of
the network of relationships can explain differences in individual success. We
focus on the nature of success as being either innovative or popular, and
derive analytical results as well as observations from computer simulations, to
find that innovative as well as popular success can be achieved by means of a
central position in a star-shaped network, but only innovative success can be
achieved by means of a central position in a scale-free network. Most
remarkably, successful individuals in both types of networks are characterized
by a medium degree, but a low out-degree, i.e. people who are well-connected,
but do not overconnect others. This observation may have important practical
implications, and could help to explain the success of individuals such as
Steve Jobs, who are able to bring together people with different talents and
skills in order to achieve something new and innovative.
  From a theoretical perspective, our work may help to answer questions such
as why individual differences in success are so large in real-world networks,
and why successful individuals tend to be successful in multiple domains. It
may also help to answer questions about the evolution of networks, such as
whether and how successful individuals are overrepresented in the next
generation of a network.
  Finally, it may be interesting to investigate to which extent the
observations reported here are general, and to what extent they depend on the
specific properties of the networks considered. This may help to answer
questions about the mechanisms that lead to the emergence of different types
of successful behaviour in different types of networks.
  In summary, this work may help to answer several questions about the
relationship between network structure and individual success, and may have
important practical implications.

the COVID-19 pandemic
affects the academic performance of students. We use student-level data from
Georgia State University and employ a difference-in-differences method to
estimate the impacts of remote learning on students' GPA. We find that
academic performance does not change significantly on average. However, we
observe heterogeneous effects. Students who are more likely to drop out
experience a significant decline in their GPA. We also find that students who
are more likely to struggle academically experience an improvement in their GPA.
Finally, we find that students who are more likely to work while taking classes
experience an improvement in their GPA. These findings suggest that (1) the
coherence of the curriculum matters, (remote learning may be more effective
than traditionally assumed if it is designed to be more modular); and (2) the
drop-out and enrollment decisions influence the extent to which remote learning
can be a substitute for in-person learning.
  Our analysis highlights the importance of accounting for students' enrollment
decisions when evaluating the effect of remote learning. We provide a framework
that can be used to investigate heterogeneous effects of remote learning in
the future. We also provide evidence that can be used to inform curriculum
design and student support policies in the future.

methods represent the relationship between data points using an edge and the

clustering, dimensionality reduction, and data analysis. Among graph

generalization of the spectral clustering's similarity matrix to represent
the geometry of the underlying manifold. To compute this representation, we

non-linear geometry of the underlying manifold. We show that our approach

works have shown how to
differentiate the solution map of a (continuous) parametrized optimization
problem, opening up the possibility of embedding mathematical optimization
problems and their solutions into end-to-end learnable models. This allows one
to minimize the distance between the two outputs from two different paths (one
via optimization and the other via a deep network), and then to use this
difference as a loss function in a training procedure. In this paper, we show
how one can use a particular class of mixed-integer optimization problems as a
building block for creating such a loss function. This involves showing that,
under certain conditions, one can differentiate over the binary variables of a
mixed-integer linear program (MILP). To do this, we introduce a new data structure
called a dynamic constraint graph, and use it to prove that one can differentiate
the solution map of an MILP with respect to the problem data. We then show how
this can be used to train a deep network, and demonstrate the efficacy of this
approach by showing how to train a network to minimize the optimality gap of a
nonlinear 0/1 integer program (with a polynomial number of constraints) using a
loss function constructed from a sequence of dynamically differentiable MILPs.
This is the first time a loss function based on a mixed-integer optimization
problem has been used to train a deep network, and it opens up the possibility
of incorporating a wide range of discrete optimization problems into
end-to-end-learnable models.
  We also show how to use dynamically differentiable MILPs in a more general
training setup, in which the network is not necessarily trying to solve an
optimization problem, but rather to generate a set of solutions that satisfy
a set of discrete constraints. This is done by defining a loss function based
on a set of MILPs, and showing how to train a network using this loss. This is
useful for ensuring that the network maps inputs to outputs that are
topologically consistent with some desired discrete structure (e.g. a
hierarchical ordering). Finally, we show how to train a single dynamically
differentiable MILP to classify a dataset, by defining a loss function that
tries to make the optimal solution of the MILP agree with the training labels.
This is useful for incorporating discrete constraints directly into the loss
function, and shows how the optimal solution of the MILP encodes the learned
features and patterns in the data.

mechanical and biochemical properties of its components. However, the
complexity of the cell hinders a comprehensive understanding and hinders the

we propose a simple dual-phase system composed of an active liquid drop resting
on a elastic substrate, which reproduces some of the main features of the cell
spreading and motility, such as the balance between the internal and external
tension, the curvature and the mechanical activity. This model allows us to
perform a systematic analysis of the phase diagram of the system, which is
presented in this work, and to gain insights into the underlying mechanics of
cell spreading and motility.

quasi-spherical, a prolate and an elliptical shape, which are characterized
by different values of the internal and external tension, and by a rich phase
diagram that can be qualitatively compared to the cell's one. In particular,
an increase in the mechanical activity is able to induce a transition from the

model that captures the strategic behavior of $n$ self-interested miners in a
blockchain system. In particular, we show that even if each miner acts
individually and only aims to maximize her own profit, the system as a whole
may still be steered towards a bad pure Nash equilibrium (NE) state, from which
no better NE can be reached. To illustrate this, we consider a case study of a
blockchain-based voting system. We show that if the number of the miners is
large enough, the system may be forced to roll back (i.e., revert) an otherwise
valid vote-finalization block, thereby compromising the system's
transactional and historical integrity. We also show that this problem can be
addressed by increasing the transaction fee, or more specifically, by
introducing a mechanism that imposes a sufficiently high penalty on the
miner(s) who cause the block rollback.

other blockchain-based systems that can be affected by similar issues.

the security and reliability of permission-less blockchain systems.

currently provide the most feasible roadmap towards large-scale fault-tolerant
quantum computation. As such, obtaining fast and flexible decoding algorithms
for these codes, within the experimentally relevant context of faulty syndrome
measurements, is of critical importance. In this work, we show that the problem
of decoding such codes, in the full fault-tolerant setting, can be naturally
reformulated as a process of repeated interactions between a decoding agent and
a code environment, to which the machinery of reinforcement learning can be
applied to obtain decoding agents. As a demonstration, by using deepQ learning,
we obtain fast decoding agents for the surface code, for a variety of
noise-models.
  We find that the learned decisions of our agents are natural generalizations
of the graph-based decoding algorithms previously obtained for these noise models,
and that they can be understood as a natural extension of the Dungen algorithm,
to the fully fault-tolerant, multi-qubit error case. Furthermore, we find that
they are significantly faster than the previously obtained graph-based
algorithms. Most importantly, we find that they can be trained to be
noise-agnostic, and thus can be used to decode even unknown codes.
  We also show how the decoding agent can be trained to make decisions based
on partial information about the code environment, which can naturally be
seen as a form of code concatenation. Finally, we argue that the use of a
particular type of neural network, that takes into account the temporal
structure of the code, can lead to significant improvements in the performance
of the decoding agent.
  We believe that the use of reinforcement learning to study the problem of
decoding topological codes, and particularly the surface code, provides a
novel and powerful perspective on the relationship between topological codes
and quantum computation. In particular, we argue that the process of decoding
the parity of a topological code provides a natural model of a computation that
can be used to demonstrate the "reliability" of the code, and that this is
closely related to the problem of obtaining an "effective" number of qubits, a
crucial ingredient of any quantum computing platform.

highly-entangled quantum states before performing single-shot measurements to
reveal information about an unknown parameter. However, in many real-world
scenarios, the full accuracy of these schemes is not required, and instead one
may prefer to use more robust and fault-tolerant procedures. Here, we consider
the problem of estimating an unknown relative phase in a two-qubit system. We
show that, when noise is present, the best possible precision that can be
achieved is the square root of quantum limited classical precision, and we
identify the quantum states and measurement strategies that achieve this bound.
We find that the optimal state is a superposition of two orthogonal states, and
we show that this result is robust to both amplitude and phase noise. We also
show that this result can be extended to the case of an ensemble of
two-qutrit systems.
  By extending these results to ensembles of systems, we show that one can
achieve the square root of quantum limited classical precision using only
classical single-qutrit measurements, provided one has access to classical
processing and adequate initial quantum resources. This is an interesting
result because it shows that one can achieve the benefits of quantum metrology
using only classical techniques, provided one has access to sufficient
initially-entangled states and adequate classical processing power.
  We show that the key to this result is to use an initially-entangled state
that is an approximate superposition of orthogonal states. We show that this
approximate superposition can be generated using only classical techniques,
and that it is sufficient to achieve the square root of quantum limited classical
precision. This is an interesting result because it shows that entanglement is
not strictly necessary to achieve the benefits of quantum metrology, provided
one has access to sufficient classical processing power.
  Finally, we show that this result cannot be extended to all scenarios of
quantum metrology problem. We show that for the problem of estimating multiple
unknown relative phases, one cannot achieve the square root of quantum limited
classical precision using only classical techniques, even with adequate
initially-entangled states.
  In conclusion, we have shown that for the problem of estimating unknown
relative phases, one can achieve the square root of quantum limited classical
precision using only classical techniques, provided one has access to sufficient
initially-entangled states and adequate classical processing power.

the most famous recursive
algorithms used in numerical computation of mathematical functions, the
Lanczos-Chebyshev algorithm, when it is implemented with a floating point
arithmetic. It is shown that this algorithm, when implemented naively with a
floating point arithmetic, does not converge to the desired function, but to
some limit function that is an analytic continuation of the original function
with a different radius of convergence. It is also shown that, due to the
different radii of convergence, the algorithm does not terminate for some
inputs for which it should theoretically terminate. Numerical examples are
presented to illustrate these results. It is also shown how some of these
illusions of nonconvergence can be avoided by using a suitable test for
termination. Finally, it is shown that, at least for the hypergeometric

deployment of HPC workloads on large-scale heterogeneous clusters. However, it
also introduces significant challenges for efficient resource management. In
this paper, we present a performance-oriented scheduling framework, called
Performance-Aware Cloud (PAC), for OpenStack-based private and hybrid clouds.
PAC provides a set of performance-oriented scheduling policies that take into
account the hardware and software characteristics of heterogeneous computing
nodes, and provides fine-grained resource management features that enable
multiple, concurrent HPC applications to achieve high performance and
efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PAC through a case study that
schedules the HPCTOOLKIT benchmark suite on a large-scale cluster deployed
using 100 nodes of the Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud.
  We show that the performance-aware scheduling policies of PAC can achieve
performance results that are comparable to those of a manual, expert-driven
deployment. We also show that the cost of the deployment can be significantly
reduced by up to 40% through automated performance-oriented scheduling. The
results indicate that PAC can be used to achieve high performance and
efficiency in private and hybrid clouds.

negation by investigating its compositionality. We focus on a particular class
of negated sentences called scalar sentences that can be true or false
depending on the level of granularity of the scalar adjective used in them.

simple statistical model that assumes a symmetric distribution over negation
can not compositionally predict the truth value of scalar sentences
comparably to a model that incorporates linguistic knowledge about the
adjective. Moreover, we show that the linguistic knowledge in the
non-parametric model is partially encoded in its predictive errors. Finally,
we show that the compositionality of negation can be exploited to improve the
predictive performance of a machine translation model that incorporates
phonetically-aware neural network modules for generating the phonology of
language.

annealed state by slow changes of the magnetization and then investigate the
corresponding probability to return to its equilibrium situation after a
quench. We find that certain annealed states can be reached only if certain
magnetic domains are avoided during the slow cooling. This leads to a
nonmonotonous probability of return in dependence on the final equilibrium
magnetization. We explain our results by a competition between the Kibble-Zurek
mechanism, which generates the structure of the domain walls during the slow
cooling, and the quenched disorder, which causes the formation of additional
magnetic domains at the annealing temperature.

semiclassical model. It is controlled by the product of two quantities: the
volume of a single domain wall and the number of domain walls, each contributing

configuration with the minimum of free energy is preferred, but only if the

be described by a mapping to a system of Josephson junctions. This allows us to
explain our findings in terms of a competition between the Josephson coupling

radiative transfer (GRT) allow one to take into account the effects of
gravitation on the radiation field within the framework of general relativity.
However, the development of GRT is hindered by the lack of a suitable model of
light geodesics that is suitable for all purposes. The existing models are
limited to small deviations in the directions of nearby photons, which is not
sufficient for the calculation of radiation fields. In this paper, we aim to
resolve this problem by deriving a new model of light geodesics that is suitable
for all purposes within the framework of special relativity and is compatible
with the classical results of Abraham and Minkowski. This is achieved by taking
a rigorous mathematical approach based on the invariant form of the equation of
light geodesics in the coordinate frame. The new model is then tested in the
context of GRT by adopting the new radiation field model that we have recently
developed on the basis of the new light geodesics model. It is found that the
new models of light geodesics and radiation field lead to the same results as
obtained by exact calculations in some cases.

long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some

known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares of other
elements of the same ring, in general, for most other rings, whether or not a
given element is a sum of squares was a mystery. In this paper, we present a
unifying solution to this problem for all commutative rings of the form
$\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $n\geq 0$, and also for some localizations of
these rings. Our main tool is a result, obtained in a companion paper, which
provides a "local" solution to this problem for the ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. We
show how this "local" result can be used to give a "global" solution for some
specific rings of the form $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Finally, using
Hensel's Lemma, we show how a local solution for $\mathbb{Z[x]}$ can be
localized to give a solution for some other rings, like $\mathbb{F_p(x)}$ or
$\mathbb{Z[2^{-1},x]}$.

show that the set of elements of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ which can be written as a
sum of squares has some interesting properties. For example, it is a

road network analysis. Road networks are often modeled as graph, where roads
are represented by edges and intersections are represented by nodes. These
models can be used for a variety of tasks such as traffic prediction, route
planning, and urban planning. As such, it is crucial to assign accurate and
reliable labels to the nodes and edges of a road network. In this paper, we
focus on the task of geolocation classification, which is a common task in
road network annotation. We experiment with several machine learning models
and find a simple and accurate solution using a multi-task convolutional
neural network (MT-CNN) with only hard negative sampling. The MT-CNN only uses
geolocation coordinates as input and outputs the road type, which achieves an
average F1-score of 0.83 on the US road type dataset. We also find that the
performance of the MT-CNN can be improved by increasing the number of nodes
with labeled road type (up to 18% F1-score improvement).
  We also find that the MT-CNN with only hard negative sampling is more
efficient (about 5x reduction in number of training iterations) and less
memory-intensive compared to a MT-CNN with all negative sampling. This is
because the number of hard negative nodes is much smaller than the total number
of negative nodes. We believe that the above findings are general and are not
limited to US road type dataset.
  To improve the performance of the MT-CNN, we propose a semi-supervised
learning algorithm, called Self-Driving Learning (SDL). The SDL algorithm
learns the training distribution from the map and uses it to select the most
representative nodes to be labeled by a MT-CNN with all negative sampling. We
find that the performance of MT-CNN can be significantly improved (up to
20% F1-score improvement) with very few (about 1%) labeled road types using
the training distribution.

geometry of the map alone, without the need for training data. This is a
surprising finding, as one might expect that the training distribution would
encode information about the US road types. We hypothesize that the common
geometry of the roads in the US is the main reason for this surprising
finding.

following intuition: instead of computing the full iteration from scratch, the

iteration and then the PS maps this local hop to the global iteration number.

independently by the clients and the PS, and (2) a "global" hop, computed by
the PS based on the sum of the local hops. We show that by carefully designing
the sum of the local hops, the clients and the PS can easily compute the
correct global hop. We show that our algorithm has a constant communication
complexity, it ensures that all clients compute the same iteration number, and
it achieves a high convergence rate, i.e., $\mathcal{O}\left(\log^2 n\right)$

be responsible for a large Reynolds number dissipation, primarily at small

various large-scale initial conditions have now been run to explore the
statistical properties of this anisotropic geostrophic turbulence, as well as
to verify the scaling of the kinetic energy observed in previous, lower

consistent with $k^{-4}$, in agreement with Goldreich and Sridhar (1993), as
well as previous rotating turbulent simulations by Smith and Pollicove (2004)
and Shew and Yecko (2006). Further, the kinetic energy density is found to
decay as a logarithmic function of the Rossby number.

turbulence. To this end, we present simulations at various aspect ratios from
very quasi-2D ($256 \times 256$) to highly three-dimensional ($64 \times 64

insensitive to the aspect ratio, but that the intensity of the turbulence
increases with the aspect ratio.

thermal Rossby number) on the anisotropic turbulence. We find that the
dissipation of kinetic and thermal energy is primarily at the same scales.

thermal Rossby number, as it does with the geostrophic Rossby number.

and that the temperature variance spectrum has a $k^{-2}$ scaling. Finally, we
find that the temperature variance is equally distributed across all

model for studying the dynamics of a discrete solid undergoing large deformations
and constitutional advection. Here, we use this model to understand how an
arbitrarily shaped particle raft moves in response to the expansion of the
underlying liquid. We derive a general formulation of this problem that is
applicable to an arbitrarily shaped particle raft and show that an
approximately closed solution can be obtained by linearizing the fluid
pressure.
  Our formulation is used to study the response of a circular, square, and
hexagonal particle raft to expansion. We find that these different geometries
have different characteristic velocities, and these can be ordered by an
effective shear modulus that depends on the geometry of the raft. The ordering
of these velocities provides a mechanism for constitutional advection that can
lead to the complete disappearance of voids and the appearance of an effective
long-range order.
  Finally, we show that this model can be used to study the sorting of different
materials that have different coefficients of thermal expansion. We find that
an initially mixed state becomes long-range ordered as the material is heated.
The use of a particle raft geometry to achieve constitutional advection in a
thermally driven system leads to a much faster sorting time than a similar
monolithic material.
  In conclusion, the use of a particle raft provides a rich and tunable model
for studying the effects of constitutional advection. This model can be used
to understand a variety of long wavelength phenomena that arise from the
interaction of an externally driven field with an internal field that is coupled
to the motion of the material itself.

several challenges faced by this class of methods. Our approach, which we call
the Global-Local TD Method (GL-TD), represents an extension of the conventional
TD learning framework to better address two of its main shortcomings: the
difficulty of specifying an appropriate set of basis functions for function
approximation and the limited capacity of these functions to capture
dynamically changing aspects of the problem environment. The basis for our
formulation is a decomposition of the value function into two components: a
global component that represents the average or typical behavior of the
environment and a local component that captures the deviations from this
average behavior. The global component is learned using a conventional TD
method, while the local component is learned using a kernel-based method that
adaptively softens the basis functions to accommodate dynamically changing
aspects of the environment. We show how our representation allows us to solve
several problems that are difficult to solve with conventional TD methods,
including multi-modal domains and domains with dynamically changing discrete
state.
  We also show how our representation provides a way to address the
exponential computational complexity of kernel-based methods by only updating
the global component at a much faster rate than the local component. To
achieve this, we introduce a new way of computing the error in the global
component that allows us to selectively update the local component only when
the global component is in error. Simulation results show that our approach
can significantly outperform a kernel-based method that updates the local
function at every time step.
  Finally, we show that our representation provides a way to solve multi-agent
domains by decomposing the joint value function into the sum of individual
value functions. We show that this can be done by assuming a particular
representation of the individual value functions that is similar to our
representation of the joint value function. Simulation results show that this
can significantly outperform a method that uses a single kernel to approximate
the joint value function.
  In summary, our representation provides a way to extend the conventional TD
learning framework to better address two of its main shortcomings. The
resulting algorithm has been shown to be able to solve a variety of complex
domains and outperform both kernel-based and conventional TD methods.

structure of the halos, and that the mass of the merger product is correlated
with the merger time scale. Furthermore, we find that the merger time scale is
longer than the Hubble time for most of the cases, which is consistent with
the non-detection of such systems in the data of the LIGO/Virvo collaboration.
However, we expect that such systems will be detected in the future with a
high probability.

dominated by the contribution of the compact object formed from the core of the
halo. This compact object can be a dark star, or a black hole, depending on its
mass and the internal structure of the halo. We find that the spin of the dark
star is typically large, with a magnitude of the spin vector of the order of
the speed of light.

nature, which is not yet constrained by the current data. Therefore, the
models of the compact halos and the merger products are highly speculative and

  The COVID-19 Severity Detection competition aims to predict the severity of
COVID-19 given the given chest CT images and patient data. The submission is
based on the score of the model on the test dataset. The task is challenging
because the training and test datasets are different. There are also many
missing values in the training data.
  To solve this task, we first train a CT image classification model to
predict the category of the given CT image. Then we train a general patient
data classification model to predict the severity given the patient data. The
final prediction is the ensemble of the above two models.
  We test different models and find that the ensemble of the above two models
performs the best. We also test different ensemble methods and find that the
simple average performs the best.

spiral UGC 8839 is known to harbour a
central double radio source. We present new observations of UGC 8839 at 1.4 GHz
with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) and previously published 5 GHz
observations with the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Combined Array for the
Millimeter-wave Observation (CAMMAP) of the University of Michigan. We detect
a central compact radio core and a separate compact nucleus offset by 2.5
kpc. The spatial separation and different properties (e.g. spectral index) of
the central compact sources suggest that they are a binary active galactic
nucleus (AGN) system. We estimate a projected mass of the putative binary
compact objects of $1.3\times10^{9}M_{\odot}$ and an estimated separation of
$<$1pc, making this one of the closest known binary AGN in the local universe.
The estimated mass and separation suggests that they are bound, and we
interpret the compact objects as a stellar-mass binary supermassive black
hole (SMBH) system in UGC 8839.

estimate that it will merge in $1.1\pm0.3$ Gyr. The merger timescale is
shorter than the typical merger timescale for the host galaxy, and thus the
host galaxy's properties will be altered by the merger. UGC 8839 is a strong
candidate for future detection of an AGN merger and we estimate that it will
be observable with the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).

altered by the merger. In particular, the merger will trigger a strong
episode of star formation and possibly a subsequent AGN outburst. The
subsequent quenching of the star formation will be delayed, and the host will
likely appear as a luminous (Luminous Virgo Galaxy, LGG) spiral in the future
rather than a LSB spiral.

possible evolution of UGC 8839 into a LGG.

The photoevaporation of protoplanetary disks, resulting from the external UV
radiation, was initially thought to be the main process responsible for their
disruption. However, the relative importance of this process compared to other
internal ones is still discussed. We present a statistical study of the
[O~III] 88.2 $\mu$m line in the sample of the PROTOSTAR Interferometer (PI) and
the Submillimeter Array (SMA) using the SOFIA instrument SPECSCAT. We aim to
assess the impact of photoevaporation in the evolution of protoplanetary disks.
We detect the [O~III] 88.2 $\mu$m line in 5 sources out of 16. The [O~III]
88.2 $\mu$m line is expected to be a good tracer of the photoevaporative flow
since its production and destruction are both directly proportional to the
electron density and the radiation field. We find that the 5 detected sources
are the ones with the highest stellar masses. We conclude that the photoevaporation
is more important in the highest mass sources, and its impact is likely to
decrease with decreasing source mass. This is in agreement with the photoevaporation
model of Merenstein et al. (2020) and in disagreement with the model of
Anderson & Adams (2006). Further observations are needed to increase the
sample and assess the results.

growth of structure in the local universe. The number of radio sources with a
given flux limit scales with the square of the comoving distance, so in a
stationary universe, the product of radio source counts with a given flux
limit and the comoving volume element should be independent of distance. We
measure this product for a variety of radio surveys, and find that it is a
monotonically increasing function of distance, with the highest redshift source
in the sample being $\sim 3$. We consider the implications of our result, and
show that a simple model in which the growth of structure is slowed at low
$z$ can fit our data. We also show that our result is inconsistent with a
model in which the growth of structure continues to the present day, but in
which the highest redshift universe is within a causal comoving distance from
us at all times. Finally, we discuss the potential for future measurements of
this type.
  We also investigate the statistical properties of our measurement, and show
that it is consistent with being drawn from a uniform distribution between 1
and 3, but is not significantly different from zero. We discuss the
implications of this result, and show that it is consistent with a variety of
models of modified gravity, but requires further observational evidence to
fully establish.
  Finally, we discuss the potential of future radio surveys to detect
correlations between radio source counts and the growth of structure. We show
that the next generation of wide-field radio surveys will be sensitive to
structure growth at $z \sim 1$, and that surveys with much wider fields will
be needed to detect such correlations at higher redshift.

definition of the quantity that we use to probe the growth of structure, to

which is based on Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). In an offline phase, the base
station (BS) first fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training samples. Thereafter, it
designs a codebook in an unsupervised manner by exploiting the GMM's clustering
capability. We design one codebook entry per GMM component. After offloading
the GMM to the user equipment (UE) in the online phase, the UE utilizes the
GMM to select the most suitable codebook entry for its UL channel. To do so, it
computes the conditional expectation of the channel (in terms of the codebook
entries) given the GMM. The UE then feedback the index of the codebook entry
with the highest expectation. In a joint detection phase, the BS receives the
feedback and projects the UL channel onto the space spanned by the codebook
entries. We propose two projection schemes; one based on the conditional
expectation and another based on the least squares (LS) optimization. We show
that the GMM-based codebook outperforms a random codebook in terms of the
achievable rate. We also show that the conditional expectation-based
projection (CEP) yields a better performance compared to the LS-based
projection. Moreover, we show that the CEP has a lower computational
complexity.

the joint detection phase. In Section VI, we present the simulation results.

scientific papers, which is added to the existing knowledge, is a major threat
to the progress of knowledge. This type of information can lead to the
elimination of confidence in the scientific community and the lives of people
can be endangered. The main reason for the spread of such information is the
lack of an efficient method for the verification of the consistency and
accuracy of the existing knowledge before adding or modifying it. In this
paper, we propose a new method based on the blockchain technology for
verifying the consistency and accuracy of knowledge. In the proposed method,
each update in the existing knowledge is converted into a transaction and a
consensus protocol is run to update the blockchain. We show that the
probability of incorrect or misleading information being added to the
blockchain is negligible. We also show that the proposed method has a
significant advantage over the existing methods. Finally, we evaluate the
proposed method through a simulation.
  We evaluate the proposed method from three different perspectives. The first
is to investigate the probability of incorrect or misleading information being
added to the blockchain. The second is to investigate the performance of the
proposed method in terms of energy consumption, transaction cost, and network
throughput. The third is to investigate the scalability of the proposed method
by changing the parameters of the consensus protocol and measuring the impact
on the network throughput.
  The simulation results show that the proposed method has a very low
probability of incorrect or misleading information being added to the
blockchain. The results also show that the proposed method has a significant
advantage over the existing methods in terms of energy consumption, transaction
cost, and network throughput. Finally, the results show that the proposed
method can be scaled up to thousands of nodes.
  In conclusion, the proposed method is a highly efficient and effective
solution for verifying the consistency and accuracy of knowledge. The method
can be used in all areas of knowledge, including medicine, engineering,
economics, and social sciences.
  Finally, it is worth noting that the proposed method can be extended to
include the deletion of transactions from the blockchain. This can be achieved
by adding a new state to the finite automaton that represents the deletion of
a transaction from the knowledge base.

the sentence similarity through a cyclic graph representation, where each

mechanism, which is further integrated into a graph-based neural network to
predict the correct dependency edges. Experimental results on three standard
datasets show that UnSupGraph achieves a new state-of-the-art performance.

the correct dependency edges for a dataset of news articles with 83% accuracy.
Thus, UnSupGraph has a great potential in unsupervised sentence dependency
parsing applications.

extract subject-verb-object (SVO) triplets from an article collection. The
user can input a keyword to search for articles that contain a specific SVO
triplet. The search is efficient, as it only processes the necessary sub-graph
of each matching article. The experimental results show that the triplets are
extracted with high accuracy and the search is fast in practice. The result
highlighting and the extracted triplets provide a great utility to the readers,
as they can quickly understand the content of the articles and also enable a
variety of downstream applications, such as ranking and summarization.

framework and provides great utility in various applications, including web

dynamics of a single charge. However, for most theories, we can linearly
combine charges, leading to an infinite number of exponentially light states.
The Lattice Weak Gravity Conjecture avoids this by fixing a particular linear
combination of charges. In this paper, we extend the Lattice Weak Gravity
Conjecture to general spacetimes by considering a family of theories with
different values of coupling constants. We find that for certain spacetimes
with non-trivial geometry, even naively single-statelike behavior requires the
dynamics to be dominated by states with energy comparable to the curvature
scale.
  We also consider a class of effective theories with modulated couplings and
find that they are able to naturally generate a large number of light states,
many of which have interesting properties.
  Finally, we use the multi-coupling Lattice Conjecture to explore the phase
diagram of $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM. By considering a family of theories with
different values of $\tau$, we find that the Higgs branch is dominated by a
single near-BPS state for $\tau \ll 1$. In this limit, the energy of the state
is exponentially close to the minimal value allowed by the conjecture.
Furthermore, the quantum numbers of this state agree with the classical
instanton that is responsible for the $a$-anomaly of $SU(2N)$.
  Interestingly, the naively single lightest state persists for $\tau \sim 1$,
but then becomes non-perturbatively heavy for $\tau \gg 1$. To understand the
full phase diagram, we find a family of near-BPS states that continue from the
Higgs branch in the small $\tau$ regime to a branch of modulated
black-branes in the decompactified, large $\tau$ limit.
  The multi-coupling Lattice Conjecture provides a rich and complex set of
constraints on effective theories. These results further illustrate the
powerful diagnostic capabilities of the conjecture and its potential to
address questions in which gauge dynamics couple to gravity.
  Finally, it is interesting to consider whether the naively single lightest
state in the multi-coupling theory could be an "almost black hole" with
dilaton-dependent effective curvature scale.
  We leave these questions and others for further investigation.

  Scheduling and trading of flexible electricity infrastructure such as
hydroelectric power plants is crucial for a changing and efficient electricity
market. A day-ahead market sets the prices and the schedules of all market
participants, and the schedules are adjusted in the balancing markets. The
scheduling and trading in the day-ahead market directly affects the overall
market efficiency and the profitability of the infrastructure and its owners.
Therefore, the market participants and the infrastructure owners need to
optimally schedule and trade in the day-ahead market.
  The main challenge in the optimal scheduling and trading is the
stochasticness of the co-optimization problem. The problem is generally
formulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MIP) and solved using exact or
approximate methods. However, solving such a large-scale MIP is computationally
challenging and may not be practical for real-time market operations. Furthermore
the general solving frameworks do not take into account the rapidly changing
electricity market and the specific characteristics of the flexible electricity
infrastructure. For example

time of the toric code plus some number of logical qubits by simulating the
associated Ising model using the parallel tempering algorithm. We find that the
mixing time grows polynomially with the code's physical qubit number. Motivated
by the connection between the mixing time and thermalization, we discuss the
implications of our results for the fault tolerance of toric code implementations
with some initial logical qubit state.
  From a numerical perspective, we achieve a factor of about 100 speedup in
computing the mixing time for the toric code with 20 physical qubits compared
to running a single trajectory with the same step size. However, the method
relies on a correct identification of when the code has thermalized and may
require large amounts of computational resources for larger codes that we could
simulate. Moreover, the results depend on the choice of initial code configuration
and whether or not we include the logical qubits in the simulation.
  We also study the toric code's autocorrelation functions to gain more insight
into the thermalization process. The spin correlations seem to decay
exponentially with the distance, with a characteristic time scale that grows
polynomially with the code's physical qubit number.
  Finally, we discuss the connection between the toric code's mixing time and
the time it takes for an unpaired mobile phase Pauli error to find another
stuck error. We argue that for the fault tolerance of toric code implementations
with some initial logical qubit state, it is the latter time that is the more
important bound.

factors provide a principled way to compare the relative strength of two
hypotheses. However, the practice of computing Bayes factors has not been
widely adopted, possibly due to the complexity of the calculations. We provide
an intuitive and computationally tractable approach to infer hypotheses in
experimental design situations. We also provide a freely available software
toolbox in R that implements this approach and is easy to use. With this
software, researchers can easily compute Bayes factors and provide interval
estimates of these quantities. We illustrate the use of this software with an
example from the cognitive psychology literature.
  Bayes factors are simple to compute for a number of experimental designs that
are commonly used in the cognitive sciences. However, the utility of Bayes
inference is not limited to researchers who are familiar with the technical
details of the calculations. Any researcher who wants to make inferences from
their data should be aware of this powerful statistical tool.
  We provide a software toolbox in the R programming language that implements a
number of Bayes factor calculations, including some novel extensions to
nonparametric tests. The software is easy to use and includes a number of
features that make it useful for applying Bayes factors to real data sets,
including data import and visualization tools, and a number of utility
functions. We illustrate the use of the software with an example from the
cognitive psychology literature (Spelke, 1990) and provide a number of
supplementary data sets that can be used to practice applying Bayes factors to
real data.
  Finally, we provide a number of guidelines for applying Bayes factors to
real data. These guidelines include: (1) make sure that the parameters of the
model are identified; (2) make sure that the prior distribution assigns
meaningful probability to the feasible region of parameter space; (3) make
sure that the prior distribution does not contain information about the
hypotheses being tested; (4) use all of the data possible; (5) consider
multiple models; and (6) be prepared to update your inferences based on the
data.

for making inferences from data. We have provided a number of guidelines for
applying Bayes factors to real data and a freely available software toolbox in
R that implements a number of Bayes factor calculations. With this software,

written and spoken language. However, they are often omitted or replaced with
different markers in different languages, which can make translation between

approach by about 20% in terms of accuracy.

for a variety of text types including news, instructions and dialogues.

studied by means of a linear stability analysis about their steady states. It

  Linear stability theory is a powerful tool to analyze the dynamics of
coupled oscillators and to explain their behavior in terms of the parameters of
the model. However, there are situations in which this approach fails. For
example, it cannot be used to analyze the dynamics of finite ensembles of
oscillators, because the steady states and the eigenvalues of the Jacobian
matrix do not exist for finite populations. Moreover, it cannot be used to
investigate the disorder in the synchronization of globally coupled oscillators
because, depending on the range of the coupling strength, either the entire
population or a single synchronized oscillator form an ordered ensemble, or
different ordered states are realized that lead to different patterns of
synchronization. On the other hand, even if the oscillators are fully
desynchronized, a small fraction of the population may be synchronized with
each other, leading to interesting dynamical states, such as clusters or
riots. Here we consider a simple model of globally coupled phase oscillators
with heterogeneous inhibitory interactions and investigate the disorder of the
synchronization using a stability analysis about the steady states that are
realized when the population is ordered. The order parameters and the disorder
diagram are introduced in the space of the heterogeneous interactions and the
results are explained in detail.

with heterogeneous interactions by considering the disorder in the sign of the
coupling. The results are obtained for a simple model in which the dynamics is
determined by a positive and a negative coupling strength. It is found that the
dynamics is qualitatively different depending on the relative strength of the
two coupling constants. In the disorder regime, the oscillators become synchronized
for a fraction of the population. The order parameters and the disorder diagram
are introduced and explained in detail. The results are compared to a model with
randomly distributed interaction strengths.

to optimise the performance of a
population of artificial neural networks on a range of tasks. We find that
significant improvements in training performance are possible, but the nature
of these improvements is complex and depends strongly on the specific
parameters of the search algorithm. We also find that the trained networks
tend to have intuitive and interpretable architectures, which is a desirable
feature in applications where network transparency is required.
  The search algorithm uses two separate populations: one to search for
networks and another to search for learning parameters (such as the
backpropagation step size) for a given network. These two populations are
linked by a mutual constraint: only the learning parameters of a network that
is of high fitness in the network population are allowed to compete in the
learning parameters population. This allows the two populations to co-evolve
in a manner that is both efficient and effective.
  We present results for two search runs, each optimising 5 different tasks.
The best network found in one of the runs has an internal error of 0.01% on a
task of size 100. This network is shown to be resistant to over-fitting and
has a learning curve that is comparable to that of a network optimised
conventionally. We also present results showing the degree to which the
optimisation process is stuck at local minima. We find that the fitness of the
networks found by the search algorithm is typically within a factor of two of
the fitness of the global optimum.
  Finally, we present results from two different regularisation schemes.
One, a simple mutation operator, proves to be effective in preventing
over-fitting. The other, a scheme based on the idea of an `off-line' error
function, is not effective.
  In conclusion, the use of co-evolutionary algorithms to optimise neural
networks has been a resounding success. Future work will involve applying the
technique to other connectionist learning systems and to other domains.

from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb collisions in terms of final-state multiplicity.
The study of Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions allows systems at similar
charged-particle multiplicities but with different initial geometrical
eccentricities to be investigated. A detailed comparison of the spectral shapes
in the two systems reveals an opposite behaviour for radial and elliptic flow.
In particular, this study shows that the radial flow does not depend on the
colliding system when compared at similar charged-particle multiplicity. In
terms of hadron chemistry, the previously observed smooth evolution of particle
ratios with multiplicity from small to large collision systems is also found to
hold in Xe-Xe. In addition, our results confirm that two remarkable features of
particle production at LHC energies are also valid in the collision of
medium-sized nuclei: (i) no significant dependence of the transverse momentum
spectra of primary hadrons on the colliding system, and (ii) an almost
conservative behaviour of the total hadron ratios.
  Finally, a new finding is presented in the form of a hardening of
transverse momentum spectra with increasing event multiplicity.
  Invited to interpret these new findings is a hydrodynamic model and
transport models including collective quantum corrections.
  None of these approaches can naturally explain the measured dependence on
multiplicity, indicating that the missing understanding of the data is not
related to the collision geometry but to the dynamical evolution of the system.
An alternative understanding of the data as due to the different
fragmentation of particles in a similar but not the same medium than in
Pb-Pb collisions is also introduced.
