investigate the dependence of hadron production on the colliding system size.
The accurate comparison of the hadron spectra in Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions
contributes to the development of reference spectra for different

finite difference and semi-implicit schemes, it shows a significant increase in

disasters taking into account the current level of the ocean, and later
publish the model with only the time of occurrence; or a company may want to
model the likelihood of sending messages as a function of the current
relationship between the communicating parties. In this paper we introduce a
new class of dynamic point process models to capture such kinds of real-world
event data. We show that this new class of models has a semi-Markovian
representation and thus applies stochastic compartmental analysis and
consequently existing results from the static multivariate point process
literature.
  We apply this model to analyze the occurrence of near-miss and fatal
head-on collisions between two-way roads. We show that the state of the roads
can significantly improve the model's ability to predict such dangerous
intersections and set the stage for future research on how to apply this
dynamic point process framework.
  Finally, we discuss some open issues such as how to estimate the parameters
of the model, how to perform statistical inference, and how to extend this
dynamic point process framework to other types of event data.

fatal collisions, two-way roads, state or context.

) have become the model of choice for a
variety of computer vision tasks. However, due to the massive number of
parameters, CNNs are computationally expensive and thus difficult to deploy
on edge devices. In this work, we propose a novel framework, called
MetaPrune, for solving the two related problems of hyperparameter tuning and
model compression at the same time using only few steps of gradient computation.
The idea is to treat the network parameters and the hyperparameters (such as
the channel number and kernel size) as one unified set of parameters and
train the whole set using bi-level optimization. The inner loop trains the
network (fixed hyperparameters) to minimize the task loss, while the outer
loop updates the hyperparameters to minimize a compression loss (e.g.,
FLOPs). Once the compression is done, we simply trim the network by removing
the unnecessary channels and the meta-layer (which contains the learned
upsampling and downsampling layers) to get the final edge model. Experimental
results show that our framework achieves superior performance (in terms of
FLOPs and model size) compared to the state-of-the-art compression methods.
Moreover, our framework is general and can be applied to any CNN model to
perform both hyperparameter tuning and model compression.

two popular models, ResNet18 and MobileNetV2, for image classification and
detection tasks. We show that our framework can reduce the model size by a
factor of 30 and the computation by a factor of 60 with only a small drop in
classification accuracy (less than 2%) and detection precision (less than
5%).

is a mathematical tool used to construct nearly
spinning superstars in numerical relativity. We investigate how different
treatment of crust physics affects the formation of spinning superstars, with
focus on the transition from the crust to the core. We consider three different
models for the crust: a finite thickness with a sharp transition to the core,
one with a finite but still very small thickness with a smooth transition, and
one where the finite thickness has a smooth transition but the pressure drops
rapidly to core pressure. For the sharp transition model, the star is too
compact and the spin is not effectively concentrated at the center. For the
smooth transition model, the spinnert behaves more like a normal star, but the
crust is still too hard. For the model with a driving term, the crust is in a
better agreement with the expected behavior, and the spinnert is more similar
to a spinning neutron star.
  We find that a smooth transition in the finite thickness model does not
result in a self-similar solution. This is in contrast to previous
calculations using the 1.5 order formalism which did find self-similar
solutions for very large compactness. The reason for this difference is
understood. The self-similar solution found in those calculations had a sharp
transition from the crust to the core, and the crust was so hard that the
self-gravity of the crust itself could be neglected, which is not a realistic
picture of a spinning star.
  We also investigate the effect of the driving term on the spinnert
dynamics. We find that the driving term becomes important only after the
spinnert has already reached high internal virialization. Therefore, the
driving term does not affect the formation of the spinnert, but only its late
time evolution.

increasing the angular resolution. However, this is not a physically
realistic explanation for the self-similar solution. On the other hand, the
smooth transition model is not self-similar, and therefore we cannot draw any
conclusions from the lack of self-similarity.
  In conclusion, the 1.5 order formalism is a useful tool for the study of
spinning superstars, but it requires a careful treatment of the crust. In
particular, the crust must be treated as a thin but still finite layer. The

and future in terms of linear correlation between two signals, \emph{i.e.},
whether the signals tend to be more correlated in the past or in the future
after a given instant. This approach is free from fixed time lags and allows
to capture the causal relationship between different types of time series. It
is also able to detect delayed causal relationships and to quantify the
correlation between signals. The method is validated on synthetic signals and
applied to the study of the causal relationship between the cardiac cycle and
the respiration in both real and simulated sleep stages.
  The results show that the proposed method is able to detect the causal
relationship between the cardiac cycle and the respiration with a high
accuracy and to quantify the correlation between these two signals. It is also
able to differentiate between different sleep stages and to detect an
activation of the respiratory system during sleep that is not captured by the
automated sleep staging. Finally, simulated sleep scenarios are used to show
that the proposed method is able to recover the causal relationship between the
cardiac cycle and the respiration even in cases in which this signal is
noise-contaminated.

that the present-day distribution of the progenitor kick is consistent with a

of health (SDoH) on the health
of individuals and communities is well-documented. However, the effect of SDoH
on the quality and safety of healthcare remains less explored. This study
investigates the impact of SDoH on hospital quality and safety by examining
the relationship between SDoH and hospital patient safety incident (PSI)
rates.
  Methods. We analyzed data from 2,534 US hospitals between 2016 and 2018,
extracted from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Hospital
Inpatient Quality Measure (IQRD) and Hospital Safety Measure (PSI) datasets,
and combined with county-level SDoH data from the US Census Bureau's American
Community Survey (ACS). We controlled for hospital characteristics such as
size, teaching status, and bed count, as well as patient characteristics
including age, sex, and race. We used linear regression to model the
relationship between SDoH and PSI rates.
  Results. We found that higher levels of SDoH were associated with higher
average PSI rates. Specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in the
Social Determinants of Health Index was associated with 0.26 more PSIs per
100 discharges (p < 0.0001). We also found that the relationship between SDoH
and PSI rates varied by hospital characteristics. For example, the positive
relationship between SDoH and PSI rates was stronger in large hospitals than
in small ones.
  Conclusion. Our findings suggest that SDoH are positively correlated with
hospital PSI rates, and that the relationship varies by hospital characteristics.
These results have important implications for quality and safety improvement
strategies, and highlight the need for hospitals to address the SDoH of their
patients.

verifications scenarios: closed domain and open domain. In the closed domain
all news to be verified are from the same dataset, in the open domain the
dataset used for training is not large enough to include all news to be
verified. The results show that a DM and a CM achieve comparable performance

the study of
stochastic complex systems. They are based on the definition of a set of
random variables defined on a given topological space, typically $\mathbb{R}^d$
or a graph. In this paper, we focus on the class of Gaussian random fields,
which is a particular case of random fields defined by an infinite Gaussian
moment generating function. We review some properties of this class of models,
such as the Fisher information matrix and the maximum likelihood estimator.
More importantly, we show that the class of Gaussian random fields is composed
of an infinite number of discrete phases, in the sense that the number of
distinct probability distributions is countable. This is an unprecedented
result for random fields, as it provides a concrete and quantitative example of
a random field with long-range dependence and an infinite number of discrete
phases.
  We show that the long-range dependence property and the infinity of discrete
phases are strongly connected. More precisely, the presence of long-range
correlation is necessary and sufficient for a Gaussian random field to have an
infinite number of discrete phases. This is an unprecedented result for
statistical models with long-range dependence, as it provides a necessary and
sufficient condition for the coexistence of these two properties in a
statistical model.
  Finally, the estimation of the number of discrete phases in a Gaussian random
field is discussed. A heuristic algorithm is proposed to estimate this
quantity and evaluated through numerical simulations. The results show that
long-range dependence and the infinity of discrete phases can be estimated with
a reasonable accuracy.
  In conclusion, this work shows that a Gaussian random field, a statistical
model with long-range dependence, contains an infinite number of discrete
phases. This is an unprecedented result for random fields and statistical
models with long-range dependence. The estimation of this quantity in
real-world data is also discussed.

computational complexity is required. It is observed that a very small number

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA) has been widely used as
an effective robust alternative to the conventional least square PCA. In this
paper, we consider a iterative reweighting scheme to solve the concave
polyhedral penalized optimization, which appears in the L1-PCA, to local
minimum. First, we propose a general algorithmic framework based on the
iteratively thresholding step for a class of such problems. Then, we show that
this framework can be reduced to a specific of algorithm for solving the
nonnegative L1-PCA to the same local minimum. Furthermore, we show that the
out-of-sample $\ell_2$-guarantee of the nonnegative L1-PCA can reach as large
a fraction $\frac{k+1}{n+1}$ of the geometric median of the data, where $k$ is
the number of outliers and $n$ is the dimension of the dataset. Finally, we
show that the proposed algorithm can be reduced to the robust PCA algorithm
suggested by [J. D. Brighten and R. Sapiro, "A statistical framework for robust
pcas"].
  The code is available at https://github.com/ChenHui2015/L1-PCA.
  The empirical study shows that our algorithm is efficient and can handle
large-scale datasets. For example, it can solve the robust PCA with $n=50000$
and $m=2000000$ within 0.3 seconds on a single desktop computer.

a supervised machine learning (ML) model. However, current pre-trained ML
models for natural language processing (NLP) contain rich semantic information
that can be used to inform the annotation process. By using the model to provide
context and to make educated guesses, annotators can work more efficiently.
This allows more and higher quality annotations to be completed within a fixed
budget. We formalize this relationship between the model and the annotation
process, and show that the impact is significant. On two different data
datasets, we demonstrate that the model can increase the yield of annotations
by 2 to 4 times, and reduce the cost per annotation by 60%. Our code is
available at https://github.com/google/nlpaub/commit/0e3c0c3f0b3c0c0c0c0c0c0}.
  We release two datasets that demonstrate the utility of using a model for
annotating data. The first is a set of 1,024 sentence-level labels for a
part-of-speech (POS) tagging model. The second is a set of 512 example-based
annotations for a coreference model. For both datasets, we show that using the
model to make guesses before looking at the full text reduces the number of
annotations needed by a large margin (3.5 times for the sentence labels and
2.5 times for the example-based labels). We release the texts, along with the
model-generated guesses and the full annotation sets.
  We show that even a simple model can significantly improve the annotation
process. While more sophisticated models may be able to do even better, the
benefits are most pronounced for models that reduce the number of annotations
needed, rather than just improving the quality of the annotations.

tools. The first is a simple web-based interface that allows an annotator to
easily view the model's output and add their own labels. The second is a
command-line interface that takes in the model's output and the annotator's
output, and returns the final dataset.

prefix-independent ones. For that we present a simple example of two
positional parity conditions whose union is not prefix-independent. We also

prefix-independent parity conditions we show two collections of conditions

conditions of the form "the first player wins if the prefix contains at least
some number $k$ of vertices of one specific color". The second one consists
of all positional parity conditions that are closed under finite unions -- a
rather surprising result.

considered in the previous paragraph.

basic operations, such as finite intersections, complementation, and
finite-to-finite mappings (which includes all restrictions and all
slices). We show that all these intersections are exactly the conditions of
the form "the first player wins if the prefix contains all vertices of some
specific set $F$". This is the same class of conditions that was mentioned
in the discussion of the first counterexample.

prefix-independent condition is equivalent to a union of several independent
linear fragments. We show that for conditions defined by a finite set of

some number $k$ of vertices of one specific color" the answer is straightforward.

polars, are of particular interest due to the complexity of their light curves
and the variety of possible interactions between the magnetic white dwarf and
its companion star. The nature of the contact or "interlocking" of the
companions in polars is still an open question, and we present here new
spectroscopic and photometric observations of the asynchronous polar, NL
Telescope, to further probe its magnetic and physical properties. We find a
spectroscopic orbital period of 173.88 $\pm$ 0.26 minutes, in good agreement
with previous photometric estimates. We also present evidence for a long
duration (about one percent of the orbital period) phase-locked emission line
burst during the binary orbit of NL Telescopii. The burst occurs in the
approach to the binary orbit's grazing contact phase and is centered on the
system's systemic velocity, and is suggestive of a stream stream interaction
between the magnetic and non-magnetic stars. The burst's duration is
suggestions that it is caused by a magnetic reconnection event in the tail of
the accretion stream. Finally, we present a new photometric analysis which
suggests that NL Telescopii's spin and orbital periods are increasing at
rates, with an interesting implication for the system's evolution.
Specifically, the difference between these two periods (the asynchronous
magnetic torque) is constant. We discuss this result in the context of the
possible degree of contact between the magnetic and non-magnetic stars.
Finally, we consider NL Telescopii in the context of a sample of asynchronous
polars and find that it shares many characteristics with other polars, but
lacks a clear polar characteristic - a sharp cutoff in its X-ray spectrum. We
speculate that such a cutoff may be present at energies just above the
capabilities of current observations.

an overview about the study of the
electromagnetic and mechanical properties of anisotropic metamaterials using
electromagnetically levitated objects as proxies. This is a developing field
where fundamental questions and open issues are located at the intersection of
physics, mathematics and engineering. Defining a rigorous mathematical
formulation for the mechanical and electromagnetic characterization of
metamaterials is a complex task due to the generality of the definition of
metamaterials and of the techniques to be employed for their investigation.
However, it is possible to outline some general considerations about the
relationship between the constitution, the electromagnetic characterization and
the mechanical stability of metamaterials. The use of levitated objects as
probes to study anisotropic metamaterials is particularly fruitful because it
allows to explore the link between the constitution of the metamaterial and
its mechanical and electromagnetic properties through a sort of "constituency
investigation". This is not a common issue in usual anisotropy characterization
where the material constitution is known a priori. In a few cases, the
relationship between anisotropy and electromagnetic suspension stability can
lead to a sort of "anisotropic bifurcation" that can be either an obstacle or
a fundamental tool for the purpose of an accurate mechanical and
electromagnetic characterization. In conclusion, the study of the properties
of anisotropic metamaterials through levitated objects can provide a unique and
fundamental contribution towards the definition of a general theoretical
framework for the investigation of these complex materials.
  From a practical point of view, the study of anisotropic metamaterials through
levitated objects requires a deep knowledge of the anisotropic properties of
the material under investigation. This is a fundamental requirement for the
purpose of a correct electromagnetic characterization and for the optimization
of the experimental conditions towards the desired goal of an accurate
mechanical and electromagnetic characterization. In this context, the lack of a
deep knowledge of the anisotropic properties of the material can be the main
cause of an incorrect or misleading interpretation of the experimental data.
For this reason, the collaboration with the physicists responsible for the
constitency characterization and the anisotropy analysis is fundamental for a
successful investigation.

agent equipped with a line-of-sight (LOS) sensor to navigate to a distant

TREC is a long-standing benchmark for evaluating information retrieval
systems, and the conference domain is particularly relevant to the interests
and expertise of many members of the UM-IU team. Our system drew on a variety
of sources, including automatic approaches developed by colleagues at the University
of Michigan, and manually selected snippets from the CDC web collection. We
describe the sources and methods that we found to be the most effective for
performing well on the conference topic set.
  We participated in the Conference Track of TREC 2021 with a diverse set of
topics and a large web collection. Our system, which we call UM-IU, performed
well, ranking 2nd in the single-topic and 3rd in the diverse-topic tracks out
of 19 submitted systems. The system performed well with both web collection
re-ranking and using web content. Looking at the experiments we conducted,
inclusion of passage ranking in addition to document ranking improved the
score by 0.14 in mean average precision (MAP) and inclusion of web content
improved the score by 0.19 in MAP. This suggested that passages were
conferring additional information that was useful for conference topic
relevance. In addition, we found that the benefit of including passages
varied by topic type with a larger benefit for single-author and award topics
and a smaller benefit for multi-author and discussion topics.
  We also found that the benefit of web content varied by topic type with a
larger benefit for discussion topics and a smaller benefit for single-author
and award topics. Finally, we found that the benefit of including passages
varied over time with a larger benefit in the early years and a smaller benefit
in the later years.

The first set of experiments looks at the effectiveness of including
conference passages in the ranking. We find that passages are beneficial for
conference topics and we investigate the distribution of benefit over the
topic set. The second set of experiments looks at the distribution of
effectiveness over time for a system that uses web content in ranking. We
find that using web content is beneficial for discussion topics and that the
benefit of web content varies over time.

metrology. Here, we propose an approach based on the measurement of the
back-action evaporation of an optical lattice trap as a sensitive method to
detect a magnetic field. The approach is based on the fact that the magnetic
field can couple two internal states of an atom to its motional state, thus
inducing a differential light scattering in a spectrum analysis. In this paper,
we first derive an expression of the back-action evaporation of the trapped
atoms in the presence of a magnetic field. Then, we show that the magnetic
field can be deduced from the measured evaporation rate. Finally, we discuss
this approach in details and show that it can reach a very high sensitivity of
the order of $10^{-12}$ T.
  From this study, we propose a possible experimental scheme to realize such a
sensitive detection of a magnetic field. The main advantages of this method is
that it is based on the observation of the evolution of an equilibrium
distribution of trapped atoms and does not require any sub-wavelength
localization of the atoms. Moreover, the use of the back-action evaporation
allows a self-referencing of the measurement, i.e. no external atomic beam is
needed. Finally, the timescale of the evaporation can be adjusted to match the
timescale of the application of the magnetic field.
  In order to increase the sensitivity of the detection, we propose to use a
\textit{anti-trapping} magnetic field along with a far-off-resonance laser. In
such a configuration, the evaporation of the atoms is enhanced and a
detailed analysis of the evaporation rate shows that the magnetic field
contribution can be easily extracted. Finally, we show that this method can
be applied to different species of atoms and that a sensitivity of
$5\times10^{-13}$ T can be reached with $^{87}$Rb and $^{23}$Na.
  We show that this method can be applied to a variety of application such as
the detection of a magnetic field generated by an electrical current in a
superconducting loop, the measurement of the magnetic field of a spinning
atom, or the detection of a single magnetic atom.

present a pedagogical introduction to one-dimensional topological phases -- in
particular the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. In the process, we delve upon ideas
of entanglement using the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix
method, geometric phase, polarization, transport signatures and the role of
Lorentz invariance. Through hands-on numerical experiments, we illustrate the
concept of a robust and quantized topological phase using a
programmable-quadrupole (a precursor to the proposed
quantum-computer Qutrit) as a central processing unit.
  We begin by introducing the SSH model and its nodal points at half-filling.
Then, we introduce the concept of polarization and show its relation to
geometric phase. Next, we introduce a charge gap by considering
next-nearest-neighbor hopping and explore transport in two limits of the
quantum computer -- the classical and the programmable modes. We show that
both methods yield the same result. Further, we discuss the role of
Lorentz invariance and how it can be used to probe topological phases using
transport. We conclude by presenting a few open-ended questions for further
investigations.
  From a computational perspective, this work is an attempt to illustrate the
concept of topological phases using a programmable device with a combination
of both classical and programmable modes. The main difference between using a
programmable device to simulate a topological model and conventional
computational resources is that the former can run faster than the latter due
to its speed and reliability advantages. Further, we show that both the
classical and programmable modes of the quantum computer yield the same result,
which is an interesting example of reproducibility in physics. The main
conclusion of this work is that a topological phase can be robustly and
quantized using a variety of computational tools and techniques.
  This work is an attempt to bridge the gap between theoretical and
experimental physicists by illustrating the concept of topological phases
using a variety of ideas and tools. Further, it is an example of how
one-dimensional topological phases can be used as a pedagogical tool to
introduce ideas of quantum computing to students and researchers alike.
Moreover, it is an example of how to develop and test a variety of
algorithms -- both classical and quantum -- to study topological phases.

alignment (GA) which is designed to alleviate three limitations of the
traditional attention model. First, the attention model only considers a

may refer to multiple places to express the same concept, such as "yesterday",

alignment between one target word and multiple source words, while it should
also model the alignment between multiple target words and multiple source

sentence, while it should also use the n-gram information of the source sentence

proposed GA model, we conduct experiments on six NMT datasets in two different
ways: one is to use the GA model as an alternative to the attention model, and
the other is to combine the GA model with other attention models to improve
translation performance. Experiment results show that the GA model can achieve
competitive performance compared to the attention model. And when combined

implemented with a few additional operations compared to a GCNN. We evaluate

non-invertible symmetries, and derive the fusion rules for the symmetries from
the worldvolume dynamics on the branes. We also explicitly demonstrate the
mapping between the symmetries and the branes for $\mathfrak{so}(12)$, and
give evidence for similar mapping for other $\mathfrak{so}(4N)$ algebras.

worldvolume fields on the branes.
  In particular, for $\mathfrak{so}(12)$, we find that the conserved charges
are related to the wound strings in two orthogonal planes.
  Interestingly, the worldvolume fields on the branes which give rise to the
conserved charges are dual to the Cartan generators of the algebra only for
certain choices of global structure, and not for all.
  This work provides further evidence for the idea that
$\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories with different algebras
may have similar features.
  We also note that the branes dual to the non-invertible symmetries can be
interacting branes, which provides further evidence for the idea that
non-invertible symmetries necessarily imply the presence of interacting
branes in the bulk.

the worldvolume dynamics on the branes provides further evidence for the
proposed mapping between the branes and the symmetries.

$\mathfrak{so}(4N)$, in particular to understand whether all non-invertible
symmetries can be described in terms of branes.

  Recurrent models are popular sequential data processing frameworks. They are
able to learn order information from the data. In this paper, we review the
following popular recurrent models: (i) Simple RNN: simple RNN is the most
basic recurrent model. It is able to learn sequential information but it is
prone to the vanishing or exploding gradient problem. (ii) LSTM: LSTM is able
to solve the vanishing or exploding gradient problem by introducing memory
units. It is a popular model for sequential data understanding and generation.
However, it is computationally expensive. (iii) GRU: GRU is another popular
recurrent model which is able to solve the vanishing or exploding gradient
problem. It is less computationally expensive than LSTM but more than simple
RNN. (iv) Bidirectional RNN: Bidirectional RNN is a framework which uses two
RNNs to learn both forward and backward order information. It is able to
effectively learn the sequential information but it is computationally
expensive.

computed tomography, deblurring, superresolution, inpainting, and other
applications. It is often the case that many image hypotheses are consistent
with both the measurements and prior information, and so the goal is not to
recover a single "best" hypothesis but rather to explore the space of probable
hypotheses. In this work, we propose a non-linear Markov Chain Monte Carlo
method for systematically exploring the region of probability density that
contains all images that are plausible under the prior and may be missing in
the measurements. We show that our method converges and demonstrate its
effectiveness on both synthetic and real data sets.
  We consider priors induced by Gaussian Markov Random Fields, and show that
our method produces samples from a distribution that is exponentially dominated
by the prior. For the case of MRI, we show that our method produces samples
that are exponentially dominated by the data-fidelity term in the energy function, and thus, by combining the data-fidelity and prior terms, we obtain a sampling distribution that is exponentially dominated by both. To obtain a sampling distribution that is dominated by the data-fidelity term, we propose a modification to the standard MRF prior. We show that this modification results in images that are more piecewise smooth, and thus, are more likely to represent real images. We also show that it results in a sampling distribution that is exponentially dominated by the data-fidelity term, and thus, by combining the data-fidelity and prior terms, we obtain a sampling distribution that is exponentially dominated by both.

properly explore the space of probable images, and thus we do not include a
description of it in this work. We include a set of open-source MATLAB code that
implements our method, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on both synthetic

superbubble, in which the impact of the superbubble on its surroundings is a
multi-phase outflow. The superbubble is produced by the collapse of a giant
molecular cloud by radiative cooling and forms in the swept-up, low-density
interstellar medium. The bubble expands until it breaks out of the surrounding
density structure, creating a hole in the density field. The superbubble and
the hole together comprise the outflow model. The hole is shown to be consistent
with observations of kpc-scale outflows. The model is consistent with the
momentum in the outflow being conserved, and we find that the kinetic energy in
the outflow is a fraction of the gravitational potential energy of the
superbubble. We find that the formation of a second giant molecular cloud from
the superbubble is unlikely, and instead the material is lost from the galaxy.
The energy in the outflow is a small fraction of the total energy in the
superbubble, and future observations will be able to test our model by detecting
the remaining energy.

phase-transition in a (Ni,Co)Ga alloy, which is modeled by a
spin-orbit-coupling and electron-phonon coupled Hubbard model. We find that
both correlations and spin-orbit coupling change the critical concentration of
Ni for the structural transition from 70\% to 80\%. This suggests that
future experiments on this alloy should be able to see the effects of
correlations and and spin-orbit coupling on the structural transition by
varying only the concentration of Ni.
  We also study the structural transition in this alloy considering
Gaussian-distributed phonon displacements. This is done by mapping the
(phonon, spin-orbit coupling, electron-phonon coupled Hubbard model to an
effective electronic model. We find that using this approach we can
reproduce the results obtained using the (spin-orbit coupling, electron-phonon
coupled) Hubbard model coupled to a harmonic phonon system. However, we find
that using a standard band-structure calculation (using the
(phonon, spin-orbit coupling, electron-phonon coupled) Hamiltonian) we are
not able to see the structural transition, which suggests that the critical
phonon amplitude to drive the transition is too large to be described by a
small perturbation of the electronic energy levels.
  Finally, we study the effect of the local electronic-phonon coupling on the
spin-orbit coupling splitting of the local density of states at the Fermi
level. We find that the local coupling to longitudinal phonon modes can
increase the spin-orbit coupling splitting by a factor of 5.
  We conclude that the (spin-orbit coupling, electron-phonon coupled) Hubbard
model is a necessary tool to understand the structural phase transition in
this alloy and that the local electronic-phonon coupling should not be
neglected when studying related materials.

evaluation is between $\mathcal{O}(\ell^3)$ and $\mathcal{O}(\ell^5)$, and
we recommend the $\mathcal{O}(\ell^4)$ order for NR simulations. We also
demonstrate how to efficiently compute the derivative of the Taylor series
expansion up to the desired order, and how to reduce the number of
time-consuming calculations. Finally, we show that the proposed algorithm can
be used to compute the retarded Newtonian potential with a similar
efficiency.
  We also show how to efficiently compute the Newtonian self-force on a
compact object using finite differences. We demonstrate that this method can
be used to compute the Blandford-Mendez shift, the spin shift, and the
dipole self-force with high accuracy and high efficiency.
  Finally, we present several examples of NR simulations where the proposed
method is employed. We find that it is approximately 2-3 times faster than the
standard method while maintaining a similar accuracy.
